full_text:
Buffalo Bills RB Frank Gore Jr. impressed against the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night, but is on the roster bubble as cutdown day nears. Bryan M. Bennett / Getty Images
ORCHARD PARK, NY — With the Buffalo Bills’ 28-27 comeback victory over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night, the preseason is officially over. With it, the on-field chances for players to earn a spot on the regular-season roster have officially expired.
All that’s left for the Bills to do is to whittle their roster down from 91 to 53 by Sunday, Aug. 30 at 6 p.m. ET. Bills general manager Brandon Beane usually tries to be as creative as possible to give himself the best chance to keep everyone he’d like.
Now with the preseason totally done, what might the final roster look like? Here is my final Bills 53-man roster projection ahead of final cuts.
The return of Allen squared as the quarterback room seemed unofficially official after Kyle Allen’s preseason showing against the Cleveland Browns, and it became official when he got Thursday night off. Even with Allen winning the backup job, it would be somewhat of a surprise if Shane Buechele wasn’t back on the practice squad.
This running back trio has no mystery surrounding it, but the lingering question is whether Johnson will be ready for Week 1. If he isn’t, whoever they keep on the practice squad is a likely candidate to be elevated early in the season. At that point, it would be Frank Gore Jr. against Ian Wheeler for the practice squad spot. Gore’s plus performance on Thursday was big for him, but was it enough to hold off Wheeler, who has looked good all summer? I give Wheeler a slight edge right now.
Waived: Frank Gore Jr., Ian Wheeler
The top five are pretty secure, so it comes down to whether the Bills would keep a sixth. With all five locks trending well health-wise toward Week 1, keeping another could be less pressing. Mecole Hardman and Trent Sherfield were both considered, but Hardman’s main draw is as the punt returner. Despite Davis muffing a punt on Thursday, the Bills at least have some safer backup options in-house in Dee Alford and Shakir. Having Hardman on the practice squad, if they can get him there, would be a good insurance policy for Davis. Sherfield, with his locker-room presence and skill set, seems like a tremendous practice squad asset throughout the season, and since he’s a vested veteran, he’s not subject to waivers.
Reserve/PUP: Tyrell Shavers Released: Mecole Hardman, Trent Sherfield, Dante Pettis Waived: Stephen Gosnell, Ja’Mori Maclin, Quentin Skinner, Max Tomczak
Even though head coach Joe Brady cast some doubt on whether the Bills might even keep a fullback on the 53-man roster, VanSumeren’s special teams ability is enough to push him onto the right side of the bubble. The other tight end decisions are pretty straightforward, with Keleki Latu a priority practice squad addition after he clears waivers.
Released: Shane Zylstra Waived: Keleki Latu
The Bills have 11 players who I believe have a legitimate chance to make the 53-man roster, so one or two tough decisions might be coming. With rookie fourth-round pick Jude Bowry in a walking boot as recently as this week, it seems like a clear opportunity to keep a pair of young players without subjecting either to waivers. In this case, the Bills would put Bowry on the in-season injured reserve list to shut him down for the first four games. Bowry looks solid in the run game but needs seasoning as a pass blocker, so this will help on all fronts.
Another projected move here is for the Bills to trade third-year center Sedrick Van Pran-Granger, who lost the backup center job to Cushenberry. Van Pran-Granger is pretty much a center only, and there are a few teams in need of center depth who could send a late-round pick for him. He was also held out of practice this week with an injury, so putting him on in-season injured reserve is another option. With those two moves, the Bills can keep Reed-Adams, who has played well this preseason, without worrying about losing him.
In-Season Injured Reserve: Jude Bowry Traded: Sedrick Van Pran-Granger Waived: Chase Lundt, Nick Broeker, Da’Metrius Weatherspoon, Bruno Fina, Sincere Haynesworth
What they choose to do with 2024 third-round pick DeWayne Carter is one of their biggest decisions this weekend. They’ve been moving Carter around between nose tackle and 4i all summer, but he hasn’t been able to nail down that backup nose tackle role well enough, leading the Bills to sign Gaines last week. With Oliver, Sanders, Jackson and maybe even Durant all ahead of Carter at 4i, Gaines being a better fit at nose tackle, plus Carter not playing on any of the core four special teams units, it might be tough to keep him.
If you’re looking for another sign, Gaines was paired only with Jackson, who is firmly on the team, and by the second half, Gaines was on the sidelines in street clothes. Carter played into the fourth quarter, which is not ideal for his chances. You have to wonder if they were showcasing him for a trade. So, with the NFL’s current craze for interior defensive linemen, they could be able to find a trade partner for Carter and recoup a much later draft asset.
Traded: DeWayne Carter Reserve/Suspended: Phidarian Mathis Waived: Zion Logue, Travis Clayton
The only slight debate with this room was Solomon versus veteran Mike Danna, but Solomon’s core-four special-teams abilities give him the big edge. Danna’s spot for the 53-man roster could have depended on Michael Hoecht’s health, but with Hoecht looking ready for Week 1, Danna is on the outside looking in. As long as he doesn’t get interest elsewhere, my guess is they’d like to have Danna back on the practice squad.
Released: Mike Danna Waived: Andre Jones Jr., Cade Denhoff
In my pre-preseason projection, I had Keonta Jenkins on the team, but a few things have changed since then. First, his preseason games weren’t quite as strong as his performance during training camp. Second, his special teams skills aren’t as strong as Andreessen’s, who the team described as a “dynamic” special teams player. Lastly, one other young player, cornerback Kani Walker, might have played too well to risk being placed on waivers. With all that written, Jenkins was my final cut. I couldn’t find a spot for him, but he’s an instant addition to the practice squad if he clears waivers.
Waived: Keonta Jenkins, Theron Gaines, Jimmy Ciarlo, Otis Reese IV
Alford and Hancock are obvious locks for the roster. Still, the real question comes down to seventh-round rookie Toriano Pride Jr., who flashes excellent athleticism but hasn’t quite nailed down a home at either nickel or boundary corner. At this point, Pride seems like a safer bet for the practice squad.
With the top three all locks, the biggest question is whether they’ll keep an additional cornerback and whether it’s Walker or Pride. Ultimately, Walker’s body of work, his fit in the defense, his size at the position and his long-standing relationship with cornerbacks coach Jay Valai (they spent three years together at Oklahoma ) give him the edge. It was also a decision between Walker and Jenkins, the inside linebacker, but with cornerbacks harder to come by and more difficult to sneak through waivers, that went in Walker’s favor as well. If the Bills wind up signing a veteran, though, Walker’s spot could be tenuous.
Waived: Jordan Dunbar, D.J. Miller, Anthony Kendall
I had Stone squarely on the roster bubble, but I think the coaching staff may like him more than we think, and enough to keep this many safeties on the active roster. Kilgore is trending toward being an early-season healthy scratch, so having four safeties they trust in Bishop, Gardner-Johnson, Hamlin and Stone becomes more of a priority. Even though this reads as six, it’s really five safeties, since Franklin is basically a special-teams-only asset and one they invested guaranteed money in with a three-year deal in the offseason.
Waived: Te’Cory Couch, Wande Owens

full_text:
Caleb Williams authored wild comebacks and stunning highlights throughout the 2025 season. Michael Reaves / Getty Images
No, they weren’t Super Bowl champions, but last year’s Chicago Bears might have been the most entertaining team in football.
With Ben Johnson on the sideline and Caleb Williams under center, Chicago churned out one long, improbable heat check. There was the Colston Loveland stunner in Cincinnati. There were two (!) heavenly strikes from Williams to DJ Moore that brought down the archrival Green Bay Packers. And there was the throw of a lifetime that pushed the Bears’ NFC divisional game to overtime.
The Bears now take on 2026 with title aspirations. Williams’ third NFL campaign begins without Moore, who was traded to the Buffalo Bills in March. But he has a young and impressive group of pass catchers comprising Loveland, Rome Odunze and Luther Burden III. The defense boasts pocket-wrecker Montez Sweat, who had 10 sacks in 2025, and two-time Pro Bowler Jaylon Johnson as CB1. While the NFC North looks like one of the league’s toughest divisions, Chicago has reason to believe that something special is on the horizon.
Accordingly, we’ve put together this broadcast guide to the 2026 season. The Bears are lined up for four primetime games in the first nine weeks, plus rivalry games on Thanksgiving versus the Detroit Lions and on Christmas against those hated Packers.
Follow the Bears on The Athletic, and keep up with our dual beat writer team of Kevin Fishbain and Dan Wiederer .
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper. The Bears’ first appearance on CBS this season comes on Thanksgiving Day in Detroit.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds Bears lifer Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC and where you can find eight Bears games this season.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside former Bears tight end Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17. The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.

title: What I learned over 4 weeks at Cincinnati Bengals training camp Joe Burrow has been lighting a fire under his team while Dexter Lawrence has been everything Cincinnati was hoping for. Paul Dehner Jr. 28
summary:
Joe Burrow has instilled a sense of urgency for the Bengals this season. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Friday’s NFL preseason action.
CINCINNATI — Since 10 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29, the Bengals have held 16 practices, one joint practice, two preseason games and opened up the locker room to the media 19 times.
It amounts to about 60 hours of direct information-gathering time at Paycor Stadium over the past four weeks. I’ve been there for nearly every minute of it.
full_text:
Joe Burrow has instilled a sense of urgency for the Bengals this season. Sam Greene / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Friday’s NFL preseason action.
CINCINNATI — Since 10 a.m. on Wednesday, July 29, the Bengals have held 16 practices, one joint practice, two preseason games and opened up the locker room to the media 19 times.
It amounts to about 60 hours of direct information-gathering time at Paycor Stadium over the past four weeks. I’ve been there for nearly every minute of it.
The general statement about the state of the Bengals is that they are in as good of shape as a team can be at this time of year.
Their issues are small, starters are settled, distractions are minimal, focus is sharp and the urgency is notable.
They look like a contender should look on Aug. 28.
It all stems from the predictions, pressure and presence of Joe Burrow.
“I’m trying to show our guys the urgency that I have, and that I want us to have as an organization to go and make it happen,” Burrow said before concluding bluntly. “I’m tired of saying next year. This is it.”
You felt the urgency and the “mean” side of Burrow every day. You saw the looks of dissatisfaction, the stomping away from an unsatisfactory rep, the words in his news conferences, the asks for extra work and the constant push for improvement from everyone around him.
“He’s been on our ass — in a good way,” center Ted Karras said. “Which is good for all of us.”
Karras noted Burrow’s leadership evolution, and he offers the ideal perspective: He’s stood next to Burrow as a captain for four consecutive years, with a fifth incoming. Karras understands how Burrow ticks and works. He also understands how that lands with coach Zac Taylor, the staff and the rest of the locker room.
The stew created by Taylor and Burrow over these four weeks produced a notable blend of intensity that hasn’t always felt that way in Cincinnati.
“This has been probably the toughest camp coach Taylor has run in my five years here,” Karras said. “I think we have the team that can handle that. We are going really hard. I think we have true, dynamic professionals on both sides of the ball.”
Dexter Lawrence took on heat for his play and conditioning during his final, rocky season with the Giants, as he rehabbed through an elbow injury sustained in 2024. Giants legend Carl Banks went so far as to say “nobody respects you,” about Lawrence on his podcast.
The comments sounded very different from the moment Lawrence arrived in Cincinnati and throughout each day of training camp. Don’t take it from the Bengals, invested in the chip on his shoulder; listen to the Chicago Bears after their joint practice.
“He’s a menace,” Bears coach Ben Johnson said, lamenting how he wrecked the practice for his offense. “He’s an issue.”
“He’s an All-Pro guy,” quarterback Caleb Williams said. “He’s a force to be reckoned with.”
Any doubt about Lawrence’s condition and impact evaporated from the first 11-on-11 session of camp and never disappeared. There can be a tendency to overinflate a new player’s value, having never seen them in this setting.
There was no overinflating Lawrence’s impact. That was partly why Karras thought this was the toughest camp in his five years.
“For me, personally, I am one-on-one with the best player in the league every single day 15-20 times,” Karras said. “It’s been a great test of my mettle, competitive stamina, endurance, toughness.”
One of the most pressing issues entering camp was the uncertain depth at cornerback behind starters DJ Turner and Dax Hill.
DJ Ivey, who has only 195 defensive snaps and zero starts, and Tacario Davis, a third-round pick out of Washington, were next in line. The nickel spot belongs to Jalen Davis, with competition coming from Ja’Sir Taylor and Bralyn Lux.
A soft-tissue injury for Hill in the early portion of camp even opened up a shot at extra snaps with the first team opposite Turner.
Ivey and Davis both stepped up and built immediate trust with coaches. Davis hit his stride over the last week. He led the team with seven tackles, including a tackle for loss in the preseason game.
Then Davis was rewarded with his first reps with the first team opposite Turner this week. He responded with multiple pass breakups against Tee Higgins and held his own against the Bengals’ star.
“Call it whatever you want to call it. I’ll say it was smooth,” Davis said, underplaying the moment and continuing a theme of humility he showed throughout August. “I don’t really set limits on myself. Sky is the limit, so I go out there, have fun, fly around, do what I need to do.”
Ivey and Davis might be unproven, but the “smooth” camp sets a foundation of trust if Hill or Turner miss time.
Dohnte Meyers might not only be the best story in Bengals camp, but the best story in any NFL training camp. This week, in the practice following Ja’Marr Chase’s injury scare, Meyers was running the first team in the star’s absence.
At first, it felt like his only path to make the club was as a returner, but the consistency of his playmaking at every turn of camp and the preseason made him undeniable. The 26-year-old was working extra after practice with Burrow on Wednesday and is a roster lock with an offensive role on opening day.
“Physically, he’s quick, he’s fast, he’s got another gear,” receivers coach Troy Walters said. “You saw that Day 1. He’s just a great kid. He comes in and puts his time in this spring. He was meeting with Davis Koetter, my assistant receivers coach, every day. Going through the plays. He made it an emphasis to learn the plays and know what he was doing. He doesn’t make many mistakes. He can play all three positions. He’s playing like a vet out there.”
Meanwhile, rookie Colbie Young made as many highlight catches as anyone, validating the Bengals’ fourth-round pick. The key will be picking up the details of the complicated offense. Walters says Young has done a nice job, but it’s a heavy ask of any rookie to come into a group that’s been together for years. Still, the seeds of a bright future were planted.
After Young, undrafted rookie Noah Thomas made plays, including a touchdown in the Bears game. Mitch Tinsley’s camp was less spectacular than last year, but the team still likes what he brings.
Andrei Iosivas’ contract will be up after this year, and the Bengals look to have rebuilt the entire back end of the receiver room, judging by the early returns.
“Last week of camp, I wanted to see guys continue to get better, get better, and they did,” Walters said. “The competition is making our decisions a lot tougher.”
The issues at offensive tackle became a theme of camp, and the team is assessing options inside and out of the building to solidify that group.
However, with the need to rebuild depth on the interior, it was an encouraging month.
Sixth-round pick Brian Parker II surprised people with how his physicality translated to guard after spending his career at Duke at left tackle.
“He had a big jump from Week 1 to Week 2,” offensive line coach Scott Peters said.
After the second game, Peters moved Parker from left guard to right guard because he’ll need to fill either spot coming off the bench.
Connor Lew enjoyed a return to football after coming off an ACL injury without setbacks and looks to be the future at center beyond Karras.
The biggest surprise, however, was finding an intriguing player in Jacob Bayer. Most known for a flowing mullet when he entered camp, he left known as a real option to provide interior offensive line depth. He was cut by the Bills last year and spent the next 10 weeks attending six tryouts before landing a practice squad deal with the Bengals.
He’s made the most of it, and Peters shifted him over to guard this week, a spot the Arkansas State product said he hasn’t played since high school. That’s a sign of respect and intrigue for the strength Bayer brought to the position. Matching that trait with Peters’ technical MMA background might have unlocked potential.

full_text:
Will Dillon Gabriel's strong performance Thursday night against the Patriots earn him a roster spot? Nick Cammett / Getty Images
The Cleveland Browns will be one of the league’s youngest teams in 2026. But most of the complications in projecting the team’s initial 53-man roster stem from lingering injury issues.
Depth for the rebuilding Browns was a concern in some spots even before injuries began to mount, but the team has multiple veteran players who barely participated in training camp. While the Browns go about the business of cutting players and preparing to explore the waiver wire, they might also consider potential trades to add experience at tight end, cornerback and along the defensive line.
All 32 teams must trim their rosters from 90 to the regular-season size of 53 by Sunday. The first run of the waiver wire is Monday, when teams can officially build their 16-man practice squads.
After a quarterback competition between Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders, the Browns will start Watson but still might keep three younger passers. There are gifted young players at running back, wide receiver and tight end, but there’s not much proven depth anywhere — and all three drafted offensive linemen could end up seeing significant playing time this season.
Based on the team’s three preseason games and four weeks of training camp practices, here’s our best guess of which players will make the initial 53-man roster under new head coach Todd Monken — and the areas in which the team figures to at least seek external help.
Deshaun Watson, Shedeur Sanders, Dillon Gabriel, Taylen Green
No one knows where this is headed. The Browns have had at least three starting quarterbacks in each of the last three seasons, and it’s not wild to believe their 2027 starter is not on the roster.
It was Watson versus Sanders all summer, and Monken wanted Watson all along. But there’s still no indication that anyone in this room can succeed. How do they construct it? That’s a mystery, too. Unless the Browns find a trade for Gabriel, I think they’ll keep four quarterbacks — at least for now.
Perhaps the team will feel comfortable exposing Green to the waiver wire and believing he can return via the practice squad.
Quinshon Judkins, Dylan Sampson, Rocket Sanders, Carsen Ryan (fullback)
Judkins is the clear lead runner, Sampson will have a pass-game role and the rest remains unsettled. Veteran fullback Michael Burton missed almost all of training camp and didn’t play in the preseason. Ryan went from playing both fullback and tight end to mostly playing fullback — with mixed results.
Even if Burton is healthy, the Browns could cut him without exposing him to the waiver wire because he’s a vested veteran. That means Burton could eventually be back. Rocket Sanders probably will make it, too, and the Browns likely have higher external priorities now. Expect undrafted rookie Davon Booth to make the practice squad.
KC Concepcion, Denzel Boston, Jerry Jeudy, Isaiah Bond, Tylan Wallace
Even after he caught two touchdown passes (and nearly a third) in Thursday night’s preseason finale, I have Luke Floriea on the wrong side of the bubble. The Browns have to address pressing needs at other positions, and I’m not sure Floriea can really help on special teams, as any sixth wide receiver would need to.
There are clear upgrades at the top. The first five is firm, and Floriea, Gage Larvadain and Malachi Corley are all in the mix. I think the Browns will want Floriea back via the practice squad and that he will eventually get a chance this season. But I can’t see him being among the best 53 right now. Perhaps I’m wrong.
Harold Fannin Jr., Blake Whiteheart, a player not currently on the roster
The Browns are in the market for a blocking-first tight end. They could even add two tight ends in the coming days after they lost two veterans to season-ending injuries.
Rookie fifth-rounder Joe Royer didn’t participate in training camp for undisclosed personal reasons, so even if he returns to the team, it’s impossible to see him contributing soon. Fannin is gifted and will be productive again, but the lack of depth otherwise has limited the team’s ability to work with its full list of eventual personnel groupings.
The starters: Spencer Fano, Zion Johnson, Elgton Jenkins, Teven Jenkins, Tytus Howard
Depth: Austin Barber, Parker Brailsford, Dawand Jones, KT Leveston
I’m projecting Leveston in and Zak Zinter out, though that easily could end up being the other way around. The Browns could even look outside for a potential upgrade. Barber seems to be next in line at right guard but also has tackle ability. For now, Jones would be the top backup tackle.
After missing almost four weeks, Brailsford was in uniform Thursday night  — with a brace on his injured thumb — but did not play. We’ll consider him a roster lock now that he’s preparing to participate again. If he’s in, Luke Wypler is probably out. The Browns could end up keeping either nine or 10 offensive linemen among the initial 53.
Maliek Collins, Mason Graham, Jared Verse, Isaiah McGuire, Derek Barnett, Mike Hall Jr., Adin Huntington, Kalia Davis, Khordae Sydnor
For now, we’re keeping the defensive ends and defensive tackles together in part because Hall is apparently going to play both. The Browns have been scrambling for healthy bodies at tackle all summer, and then lost starting defensive end Alex Wright to a season-ending injury last week. That prompted the addition of Barnett, a 10-year veteran.
The Browns had already been seeking another experienced pass rusher, and they’ve tinkered with using Hall on the edge in certain situations. Davis is the toughest projection because he hasn’t participated since the first day of camp, while Sydnor is an undrafted rookie worth tracking. He played on the first kickoff and kickoff return teams in the preseason finale.
Logan Fano, Spencer’s brother and the team’s other undrafted rookie defensive end, suffered an injury on the final series of the preseason finale. If he’s healthy, he’ll likely be cut and then land on the practice squad.
Carson Schwesinger, Quincy Williams, Winston Reid, Easton Mascarenas-Arnold, Justin Jefferson, Nathaniel Watson
Schwesinger and Williams are the clear top two. Reid and Mascarenas-Arnold played as starters in August because Schwesinger was dealing with a minor injury — and because the Browns wanted to evaluate them.
The last two spots will be special teams-only players for now, but the team could continue to look for upgrades. Watson can probably be grouped with Zinter, Leveston, Larvadain and Floriea (and some others) as true bubble players, as general manager Andrew Berry explores potential trades and decides which players the Browns don’t want to expose to waivers.
Denzel Ward, Tyson Campbell, Myles Harden, Mekhi Blackmon, Tre Avery, a player not currently on the roster
Two top-level starters, one more lock … and a bunch of questions. The Browns were hit hard by injuries in training camp and never had any of their journeymen veterans separate themselves from the options at the bottom of the roster.
Blackmon was claimed off waivers Thursday, so while it’s too early to know what role he might have, he’ll be on the roster next week. Undrafted rookie Michael Coats Jr. had a strong camp but wore a protective boot on his right foot Thursday night. It’s hard to project Coats without knowing more about his injury, but it’s not hard to guess the search for more external help will continue.
Grant Delpit, Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, Ronnie Hickman, Donovan McMillon
The Browns have a clear top three, and McNeil-Warren is talented but raw. He’ll probably play sooner rather than later, while McMillon seems to have earned a job for the second straight summer.
Veteran Daniel Thomas is in the mix for a special teams job, but he was among the players who missed the preseason finale due to injury. We can’t project him landing on the initial roster without a clearer forecast, but he could eventually…

The Athletic Football Show is previewing all 32 teams leading up to the start of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Dallas Cowboys. The quotes are edited for clarity. You can watch the whole preview on YouTube and in the embedded video below, or listen to the full NFC East preview wherever you get your podcasts.
Derrik Klassen on what about the Cowboys most excites him: This might be the best offense in football. I just feel that they have all the right pieces. They have a quarterback who we’ve seen play at MVP heights before and put up some of the best passing numbers in the NFL. They have an offensive line that is young and really talented almost across the entire board. They have, outside of Cincinnati, the best one-two punch at wide receiver in the NFL. The offensive line was exciting last year, but they were a little bit banged up and a lot of those guys missed time. It wasn’t that many games, but when Tyler Guyton and Cooper Beebe played together, they had a 45.2 percent rushing success rate, according to TruMedia, which would have been tied for third in the league with the Chicago Bears. When they had their guys, they were mashing people. If they can get back to that in the second year in the system, this could be wheels up.
Robert Mays on what he’s watching the first month of the season: Can Christian Parker do this? People have said that I’m baking in an improvement from the Cowboys defense and how we talk about them, where I would typically be more speculative with a first-year play caller in other situations. I’m absolutely doing that. We collectively play the wait-and-see game so often on this show. And we do that because we understand the things we don’t know. But every once in a while, if you believe in something, if you have conviction about something, make a stand. I haven’t been shy about this. He’s got the goods and I think that they can do it. And yes, I’m baking that in a way that I wouldn’t with a coordinator I’ve never seen do this before.
Dave Helman on what’s keeping him up at night: We’ve been talking about it for two weeks, but at this point, across the NFL community, the defensive turnaround feels like a fait accompli. The Cowboys being a trendy Super Bowl pick because of a defensive turnaround that feels plausible but is entirely theoretical keeps me up at night.
I undermined myself a little bit when I looked at the DVOA stuff and saw that there’s plenty of precedent for units doing this. It’s not nuts. That doesn’t mean it’s going to happen. And for all the teams I said had these big turnarounds, there were plenty that went from 31 to 27 or 32 to 24, and 24 is not going to be good enough to get where you’re trying to go.

full_text:
Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb headlined an elite offense in 2025. Stacy Revere / Getty Images
Once again, the Dallas Cowboys arrive fresh off an eventful offseason with deep playoff aspirations. In other news, Texas is hot and Frito pie is filling.
It’s an evergreen sentiment under Jerry Jones, of course, but this feels like a massive year for the glamour franchise. Dallas still hasn’t reached the NFC Championship Game since the days of Troy Aikman, Michael Irvin and Emmitt Smith. As expected, the Cowboys’ brass has made another conspicuous push to change that.
Playmaking wideout George Pickens is back on the franchise tag. Wrecking ball DT Quinnen Williams returns on a three-year extension, vindicating the team’s midseason trade last November. First-round draft pick Caleb Downs takes the field with Defensive Rookie of the Year buzz, as veteran edge rusher Von Miller makes a late-career homecoming. With Dak Prescott in the pocket and CeeDee Lamb in open space, the 2026 Cowboys figure to be one of the NFL’s most interesting outfits.
It remains to be seen if all that hype will convert to January or February football. Regardless, Dallas is going to be a TV staple across the regular season, currently with six primetime games on the schedule and several others available to a nationwide audience. Brian Schottenheimer’s squad starts the season on “Sunday Night Football” against the rival New York Giants, then travels to Brazil alongside the formidable Baltimore Ravens in Week 3. The annual Thanksgiving home game brings on the hated Philadelphia Eagles. Cups runneth over.
Keep up with the team on The Athletic feed, and follow Jon Machota as he traverses the Cowboys beat.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. The Cowboys will play in two of them — their first is the Rio de Janeiro showdown against the Ravens. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC and where you can find eight Cowboys games this season, including the Thanksgiving Day clash with the Eagles.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who was recently inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN — including Dallas’ two MNF appearances — while another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17.  The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by Cowboys hero Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Among the pregame and postgame personalities are former All-Pros Tony Gonzalez, Richard Sherman and Andrew Whitworth.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.

full_text:
Jonah Coleman runs the ball during a preseason game against the Falcons. Danny Karnik / Associated Press
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — Jonah Coleman never attended a San Francisco 49ers or Oakland Raiders game as a kid growing up in Stockton, Calif. Though he attended the University of Washington, across town from Lumen Field, he never took in a Seattle Seahawks game, either.
So Coleman, the running back the Denver Broncos selected in the fourth round of April’s draft, attended his first NFL game while making his debut in Denver’s preseason opener in Atlanta on Aug. 14.
“I had never really thought of it that I hadn’t been to (an NFL) game,” Coleman said this week in a quiet corner of the Broncos’ indoor practice facility after he shucked off his shoulder pads. “As time goes by, I just realized, ‘I’ve never been to a game,’ so being in the NFL was crazy. The nerves were definitely hitting me kind of hard.”
Not that anyone could tell by watching Coleman in his debut that night at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. It wasn’t just the 24 yards on four carries that stood out. It was the smooth decisiveness in his cuts. The physicality he displayed while taking on defenders. The generally calm demeanor that led to coach Sean Payton’s observation, near the start of training camp, that he didn’t “feel rookie” when it came to Coleman.
It turns out that’s the exact impression Coleman was trying to make when he first showed up at the Broncos’ facility for workouts ahead of a rookie minicamp in May, powered by a two-word motto: “Be undeniable.”
“I just had the mindset of, ‘I’m trying to make the team,'” Coleman said. “So I’m trying to do everything right, trying to stand out. The biggest thing is trust coming in as a rookie. So just trying to gain the coaches’ trust, gain my teammates’ trust. They ain’t going to put you in the game if they don’t trust you, so it’s just doing the little things right and being undeniable.”
His experience in Jedd Fisch’s pro-style system at Washington gave Coleman a head start in some areas critical to gaining Payton’s trust as a rookie running back. The Huskies played with an up-tempo style, running backs coach Scottie Graham said, that kept Coleman on the field on all downs. So his role demanded that he be a capable receiver and a trusted wall in pass protection, able to recognize blitzing patterns.
“He did a number of things on tape or was exposed to certain protections maybe that a lot of college backs weren’t. So you feel an older player or a veteran player, and you saw that on tape. … You had a chance to see more of it maybe than you do with some other guys,” Graham said.
The most significant impact Coleman may have this season, though, is as a between-the-tackles complement to starter J.K. Dobbins. Broncos assistant general manager Reed Burckhardt said after the draft that comparisons of Coleman’s running style to that of the veteran Dobbins were “valid,” and that could give the Broncos an opportunity to lessen Dobbins’ rushing load with the aim of keeping him healthy throughout the season. RJ Harvey scored 12 total touchdowns as a rookie last season and has looked in this camp like a player who can be Denver’s most dynamic receiving threat at running back since Knowshon Moreno caught 60 Peyton Manning passes in 2013. But Coleman, a tackle-breaking force at Washington, could be a better fit as an interchangeable piece with Dobbins on run downs.
“He runs the ball really well. A lot of guys want to come in and be something else other than a running back,” Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton said. “As a young guy, it’s like, focus on inside zone, outside zone, making the right cuts. In this league, it’s hard to be patient and find the right spots because guys are so much faster. No matter where you went to college, maybe one or two guys from that team get drafted or even as undrafted (free agents). Out here, it’s every guy from every one of those teams, so to see him be able to feel that and be a patient runner and then attack it every time has been special to see. Every time we’ve seen it live, like in the preseason, he’s taken another step each week.”
Coleman said he learned early while operating within Denver’s offense that “one little step, one little misalignment, can mess up everything that was supposed to happen on that play.” He is running against a Broncos defensive line in practice that erases nearly all margin for error on most plays. That’s why Coleman’s work behind the scenes may best explain why he’s put himself in a position to grab a significant role in Denver’s offense from the start of the season. Broncos running backs coach Lou Ayeni said Coleman “is a guy who doesn’t back down from the competition,” and that has been illustrated by the way the 22-year-old has challenged himself to grasp the concepts in the deepest corners of the team’s playbook.
“We have thrown a lot of installs at him and he’s been great with that,” offensive coordinator Davis Webb said.
Coleman, of course, is one piece of a backfield that Payton says could be the most complete since he took over as the team’s coach in 2023. Dobbins, who was fifth in the NFL in rushing when he went down with a season-ending foot injury in Week 10 (772 yards), is pivotal to Denver’s hopes of being a more consistent and explosive offense. The veteran is fully cleared of a soft-tissue injury that nagged him early in camp and put together one of his top practices of training camp on Wednesday. Coleman said having a player like Dobbins as the vet in the room has been invaluable — if demanding.
“He’s really hard on me, so anytime I’ve got a question or anything, I’m able to go to him and talk about it,” the rookie said. “Or if he thinks that I need to do something better or pick up the tempo or just anything that I need to fix, J.K. is the first person to tell me. Like, ‘Hey, man, you’ve got to hit that!’ Or, ‘Hey, man, good run!” He’s just picking at extra details and being hard on me because he wants us to be good. He does that to everyone in the running back room and that’s great to be around.”
Coleman has indeed made his spot on Denver’s roster undeniable. All that remains to be seen now is how quickly an offseason that drew praise from coaches and teammates alike can translate to a role that helps elevate the Broncos’ offense.

full_text:
Linebacker and special teams contributor Joe Bachie has been reliable and has made plays this preseason, coach Dan Campbell says. Is that enough to make Detroit's 53-man roster? Paul Barnick / Imagn Images
The preseason finale is almost here, and as soon as it’s done, coach Dan Campbell and general manager Brad Holmes have decisions to make. They’re on a deadline.
The Detroit Lions will travel to Indianapolis on Friday, face the Colts on Saturday and have a completed roster by 6 p.m. ET Sunday. A quick turnaround that doesn’t leave much time for thorough evaluations.
“I mean, this is difficult,” Campbell said. “You have got to have a pretty good idea where you’re at before you go into that game, knowing there’s a few spots left. But you better have a pretty good idea because it’s a quick turnaround. We land next morning, get up, and we’ve got things we have to do and it’s difficult.”
That said, here’s a look at a few players who could help themselves in the finale — hoping to leave Holmes and Campbell with a lasting impression before cutdown day arrives.
The QB2 competition rolls into the final week of the preseason. At this point, it’s a matter of preference. Do the Lions prefer an experienced veteran who can help Jared Goff prepare for upcoming opponents and offer an extra set of eyes on the sideline during games? Or would they prefer the upside of a developmental QB like Altmyer — who’s shown the ability to manage a game in the preseason and limit turnovers?
If Dobbs has another game where he looks like he’s doing too much and putting the offense in a bad position, it’ll hurt his chances. He’s got the leg up right now, but his interception versus the Washington Commanders was an ill-advised throw. While Altmyer is subject to waivers (unlike Dobbs), there’s a good chance the Lions can keep him around on the practice squad and continue to invest in him without burning a roster spot on an inexperienced QB2.
Signed midway through training camp, Stille has worked his way into the roster mix. He’s made plays seemingly every practice — whether it’s a sack, a run stuff or taking on a double team. He offers positional versatility and has the size to compete inside. If the Lions go heavier at defensive line, it could come down to Stille and Chris Smith. I’d give the edge to Stille right now, based on what I’ve seen.
“He’s a pro, smart, really smart,” Campbell said of Stille. “He’s got versatility, very strong. He can shed blocks, shock, make plays, kind of knows himself, knows what he is, knows his own limitations and can play fast enough to cover up for some of those. But that’s what the intrigue with him is — the versatility, man. … The more you can do and the more that you can prove you can do, that is always going to help your case.”
The Michigan State alum has been a mainstay with the second-team defense and offers value on special teams, playing 200 snaps there in each of the last four seasons. He has quietly had a strong camp and could work his way onto the roster, especially if rookie fourth-round linebacker Jimmy Rolder needs more time before he returns to practice. Bachie and Campbell crossed paths with the New Orleans Saints. Campbell is high on him.
“Just a smart, crafty, all-out linebacker,” Campbell said. “He just picked up where he left off from when I remember him. I mean, that’s what he’s been in this league and he’s walked in the door and he’s got a great grasp of this defense right now. And he can play on special teams and do anything that (Lions special teams coordinator Dave) Fipp’s asked him to do. So, he’s pretty dependable. He’s reliable and he’s made plays in camp.”
Meeks was a popular choice to make the roster last week , when Sam LaPorta’s status for Week 1 against the Saints was unknown. Meeks is coming off an excellent preseason game against the Commanders, which gives him momentum heading into the preseason finale. However, LaPorta returned to practice this week and picked up where he left off. There aren’t many signs of rust or injury there — great news for LaPorta and the Lions, less great news for Meeks’ chances of making the team. There’s still a chance the Lions like Meeks enough to roster four tight ends, joining LaPorta, Brock Wright and Tyler Conklin. But it’s hard to imagine a team using a waiver claim on an inexperienced second-year wide receiver-turned-tight end, so chances are Meeks could be stashed on the practice squad.
It sounds like Isiah Pacheco (knee, back) might not be ready for the season opener. Campbell said the sprained MCL he suffered earlier in camp is not the concern right now — it’s a back injury he picked up. Now, the Lions may prefer to add a veteran running back (they worked out Kareem Hunt this week) rather than keep a back like Smalls. He’s admittedly a roster long shot. However, Smalls knows the offense, he’s already with the team and has a chance to stick around on the practice squad. An elevation makes sense if Pacheco misses time early in the season, but only if he proves his value.
Campbell wants more consistency out of Lovett, which is worth noting when factoring him into roster plans. If the Lions are going to keep a fifth or sixth receiver, that receiver must be dependable — be it on offense or special teams. A guy like Tay Martin has been praised by this staff throughout the offseason for his reliability on special teams. Lovett hasn’t earned that sort of love on special teams or offense. And while he made the roster last year, if not for an injury to rookie WR Kendrick Law (torn ACL), Lovett would be on the outside looking in. He’s got a chance to impress Saturday, but needs to make a splash one way or another.
When camp began, Bartch was a dark horse to start at left guard. Signed by the Lions this offseason, Bartch was expected to compete with Christian Mahogany for the starting left guard job. At times, he’s repped with the first-team offense, but he’s missed more practices with injuries than he’s participated in, and Campbell admitted he’s running out of time to get back into the mix. Mahogany has been the starting left guard all week. Barring an unforeseen change, he’ll be the Week 1 starter.
That said, it doesn’t quite feel like this is over. Bartch’s return to practice this week was a welcome sight. He needed to get his feet under him and string together performances, which he’s done this week. He can continue to do so Saturday — shaping up to be his first game action this preseason. As things stand, Bartch is the next man up at guard if there’s an injury to Tate Ratledge or Mahogany. You also can’t rule out a starter change if Mahogany struggles early in the season. Bartch has fans in the building.
At this point, Juice Scruggs is the Lions’ projected starting center. He’s the first center out with the No. 1 offense in practice, and that was the case when he suited up for his first preseason game against the Commanders. We’ll see if McLaughlin plays Saturday after missing Thursday’s practice. If he does, it’ll be his last opportunity to make the team. He’s had nice moments, but others where he’s been overmatched.
McCreary’s had a bit of a strange camp. When practice first began, he’d often be on the wrong end of a highlight-reel catch or explosive play. He was losing one-on-one battles, was repping with the second-team defense, and it was becoming tougher to envision him on the roster.
Over the last few weeks, however, McCreary has picked it up. He’s been great in the preseason, he’s held his own on reps against these Lions wide receivers and has found a groove. When you look at the secondary depth without him — with guys like Ennis Rakestraw Jr., Keith Abney II and Nick Whiteside, among others — there isn’t much experience. And now that projected starting nickel Christian Izien is expected to miss time, McCreary’s value continues to rise. He can solidify a roster spot with a strong finish Saturday.

full_text:
Trey Lance is a huge threat with his legs, which gives him an edge in the quarterbacks competition. Harry How / Getty Images
The Los Angeles Chargers lost to the Los Angeles Rams 20-18 on Thursday night to cap their preseason.
Coach Jim Harbaugh and general manager Joe Hortiz must trim the roster from 91 players to 53 players by 3 p.m. PT Sunday.
Here is my 53-man roster prediction.
Uiagalelei closed the gap this training camp and preseason, but the Chargers will decide whether Lance gives them a better chance to win if they have to play a backup quarterback. Lance is a huge threat with his legs, and that valuable skill gives him an edge in this competition. Uiagalelei has impressive arm talent. This could be an even tighter battle in a year.
Who’s out: Jaret Patterson, Amar Johnson, Gregory Desrosiers
Desrosiers was flashing throughout the preseason as a runner and on special teams. On Thursday night, he broke out with 118 rushing yards on nine carries. Between his coverage ability on punt team and his comfort level in attacking the edges as a runner, he should find a spot on the practice squad. The top three here feel firmly set. Mitchell has been dealing with an injury, but the Chargers have more than two weeks before they open their season against the Arizona Cardinals on Sept. 13.
Who’s out: Dalevon Campbell, JaQuae Jackson, Sincere Brown, Devonte Ross, Liam Clifford, Gary Jennings
Davis is a game-breaking returner when healthy, and that will earn him a spot on the roster as the sixth receiver.
Who’s out: Scott Matlock, Jerand Bradley, Evan Svoboda, Johnny Pascuzzi
No surprises here. This group is far more athletic than in recent seasons. Matlock was inconsistent this preseason. I don’t see room for him on the roster.
Who’s out: Trevor Penning, Logan Taylor, Alex Harkey, Laekin Vakalahi, Josh Kaltenberger
World, an undrafted free agent out of Oregon, should transfer to reserve/NFI on cutdown day. He will, in all likelihood, have a redshirt year in 2026 as he recovers from a knee injury he suffered at the end of the college season. The Chargers should be able to bring back Penning to the practice squad. Logan Taylor is the tough one. He’s shown some promise at tackle in the preseason, but I needed this spot on defense.
Who’s out: TeRah Edwards, Jahmeer Carter, Jacobian Guillory, Terry Webb
Edwards pushed for a roster spot earlier in the preseason, but he didn’t have a good showing in Week 2 against the San Francisco 49ers, which sank his chances of making the roster. Eboigbe looks like a vastly improved player who could turn some heads. Barrett looks capable of making an impact as a rookie as a pass rusher and run defender.
Who’s out: Nadame Tucker, Garmon Randolph, Andre Carter
Kennard got hurt last week against the 49ers. Teams can place up to two players on injured reserve on cutdown day, and those players are eligible to return after four games. Kennard is headed there. Tucker entered camp with a shot for the 53-man, but he has not shown enough to earn a spot.
Who’s out: Junior Colson, Emany Johnson, Lander Barton
This might be the Chargers’ deepest position on the roster. In the end, they could move on from Colson, whom this regime drafted in the third round in 2024. Colson did have a pick six against the 49ers, but he is just lacking some urgency and physicality as a run defender. The Chargers could trade Colson before cuts. Something like a conditional seventh-round pick in return could make sense.
Who’s out: Noah Avinger, Devin Grant, Myles Purchase
The top five on this list are set. Williamson will earn a spot as one of the Chargers’ best and most important special teams players. Six safeties is a lot. At the same time, James moves around quite often and, as a result, can be viewed as a cornerback and a safety.
Who’s out: Eric Rogers, Rodney Shelley, Isas Waxter
Shelley has been firmly in the mix, but Smith has outplayed him in training camp and the preseason. Reed has built-in equity from his 2025 season with the Chargers. I have some concerns about this group. The Chargers will be active on the waiver wire and trade market to try to add to this group in the coming days.
Who’s out: LS Peter Bowden
Scott had a preseason to forget between his non-tackle attempt in Week 2 and his 20-yard punt Saturday night. All will be forgiven if he performs on Sept. 13.

The preseason is over, and that means crunch time has arrived for the Los Angeles Rams to decide their 53-man roster.

full_text:
With Tutu Atwell rejoining the team via trade, the Rams could have quite a few receivers and tight ends on their final roster. Sean M. Haffey / Getty Images
The preseason is over, and that means crunch time has arrived for the Los Angeles Rams to decide their 53-man roster.
Cutdown day is Sunday, and the Rams have a more straightforward roster than many teams after returning nearly every starter from last season’s NFC Championship Game loss, give or take a trio of big-name additions.
However, the roster has also gotten bloated at a few positions, making it challenging to decide which players to keep and which to expose to waivers before building the 16-man practice squad.
This season’s roster is a moving target, as the Rams are bracing for the potential of two starter suspensions, have a pair of roster locks currently working back from injuries and also have a former three-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year they could need to save a spot for.
In: Matthew Stafford, Stetson Bennett, Ty Simpson
The Rams have made it clear they are keeping three quarterbacks again, and Bennett will likely take the backup role Jimmy Garoppolo held the past two seasons. That would set up Simpson to sit and learn as a rookie, which the Rams see as valuable given the position’s complexity.
If Stafford were to suffer a significant injury, the Rams could consider calling Garoppolo, who is currently a free agent and has been contemplating retirement. If it’s a short-term injury, Bennett seems likely to be the replacement, but it’s not as settled a spot as it has been in recent seasons.
The Rams like what they’ve seen out of Caldwell this training camp, and he should be one of their practice squad additions if he clears waivers as expected.
In: Kyren Williams, Blake Corum, Ronnie Rivers
Out: Jordan Waters, Dean Connors
The Rams cleared up this position on Thursday by trading Jarquez Hunter to the Miami Dolphins for Tutu Atwell. They should roll with just three options to start the season, with Williams and Corum in a timeshare of carries and Rivers serving as a versatile special teams player who is adequate as a rusher, receiver and pass protector.
Waters and Connors impressed this preseason and should be options for the practice squad if they aren’t claimed by other teams on waivers.
In: Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, Jordan Whittington, Konata Mumpfield, Xavier Smith, Tutu Atwell, CJ Daniels
Out: Alex Bachman, Tru Edwards, Brennan Presley, Tyler Scott
The Rams made a surprising trade by re-acquiring Atwell in the deal that sent Hunter to the Dolphins. That addition adds a needed speed option and could cover a potential suspension of Nacua under the league’s personal conduct policy. Either way, Atwell, on a $1.075 million contract, is easier to treat as a luxury than when they did so last season with him on a $10 million deal.
Whittington and Smith became roster locks when the Rams gave them steady special teams roles, and they’ve been impressed with the growth of Mumpfield in his second season, including as an option on special teams.
Daniels has had a busy preseason and training camp but might struggle to see the field early with how many options the Rams have. The team also has to brace for potential load management and missed games for Adams, who still looks great but is 33 and managed several lower-body injuries last season.
In: Terrance Ferguson, Colby Parkinson, Tyler Higbee, Davis Allen, Max Klare
Out: Mark Redman, Dan Villari
The Rams are leaning into three-tight end sets even more than last season, when they discovered it midseason and led the league in that usage by a wide margin. That helps explain the second-round selection of Klare, and this group is deep enough that he could see several healthy scratches — like Ferguson did last season — until the Rams have an injury.
Ferguson should be a featured option after a year of learning the playbook and an offseason of trimming body weight and learning several different alignments, positions and route combinations. Allen missed time in training camp with a quad injury but should be ready to go by Week 1.
In: Alaric Jackson, Steve Avila, Coleman Shelton, Kevin Dotson, Warren McClendon Jr., David Quessenberry, Justin Dedich, Beaux Limmer, Keagen Trost, Blake Hance
Out: AJ Arcuri, Dylan McMahon, Bill Murray, Bryce Henderson, Wyatt Bowles, Austin Blaske
The Rams would ideally proceed with nine offensive linemen, but injuries to Trost and Dedich have muddied the picture, as has a potential looming suspension for Jackson. It makes sense to create extra space at tackle, given the questions facing Jackson and Trost and the fact that Quessenberry is 36. Once those situations stabilize, Hance could depart to make room for a third center.
Offensive line depth remains the biggest question mark for this team, given how strong the starters are and how one injury or suspension could create major risk for a 38-year-old pocket quarterback managing a degenerative back injury.
In: Myles Garrett, Kobie Turner, Poona Ford, Byron Young, Tim Keenan, Tyler Davis, Josaiah Stewart, Braden Fiske, Desjuan Johnson, Wesley Bailey
Out: Ty Hamilton, Devean Deal, Tomon Fox, Darryl Peterson III, Payton Zdroik, Bill Norton, Jaxson Moi, Larrell Murchison
This is such a deep and loaded group, and that’s before the Rams factor in a spot for a potential Aaron Donald return. If and when that happens, Johnson or Bailey likely gets the boot. Bailey is a wild card, as he flashed in ways few saw coming this preseason, and the Rams have to know they won’t get him back if they expose him to waivers.
In: Nate Landman, Omar Speights, Grant Stuard, Shaun Dolac
Out: Nikhai Hill-Green, Elias Neal, Monty Rice
This was another fairly set group from the start of training camp. Landman established himself as a leader last season and earned a three-year, $22.5 million extension. Speights should start in base but will likely be subbed out on passing downs for lots of dime personnel. Stuard and Dolac will lead and be key players on the special teams coverage units.
In: Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Emmanuel Forbes Jr., Josh Wallace
Out: Cam Lampkin, Steven Gilmore, Nyzier Fourqurean, Al’zillion Hamilton, Alex Johnson
The Rams overhauled this group in the offseason by acquiring McDuffie and Watson, and McDuffie’s All-Pro abilities at outside and nickel cornerback should add versatility. Forbes should be a better fit as a No. 3 outside option who sees playing time in dime personnel. Wallace has been training as an inside and outside cornerback in addition to safety work.
Lampkin was a difficult cut, but the Rams are overly deep at the nickel spot, which is his primary position. This would be a spot they’d need to load up on through the practice squad.
In: Quentin Lake, Kam Curl, Kam Kinchens, Jaylen McCollough
This is one of the Rams’ strongest position groups, so they didn’t have any spots to be won. Lake is a hybrid cornerback-safety who will be the team’s primary nickel corner. Expect to see Curl move to more spots this year after inking a three-year, $36 million extension. Kinchens has a chance to be a breakout player, with his ball skills behind this pass rush.
Cook should be a player the Rams try to get back on the practice squad, given his strong preseason and connection to defensive backs coach Jimmy Lake.
In: Harrison Mevis, Ethan Evans, Joe Cardona
International pathway player: Jack Bouwmeester
For all of last season’s woes on special teams, these positions were set with few worries through training camp. Mevis locked the kicking role down with his performance last season, when he made 18 of 19 field goals and a game winner in the divisional round against the Chicago Bears.
Evans had a strong start to last season, and the Rams hope they’ve tightened the coverage and blocking units to bring more out of him. Cardona began his career under new coordinator Bubba Ventrone in New England and brings 11 years of experience.

full_text:
A recent addition to the Raiders, Dare Ogunbowale (right) might stick on the initial 53-man roster. David Becker / AP
LAS VEGAS — The next few days will define the summer of the Las Vegas Raiders’ pro personnel staff.
They’re the people in charge of shrinking the roster down from the current 89 players to 53 by 3 p.m. Pacific on Sunday. And for a rebuilding franchise like the Raiders, those decisions could have a long-lasting impact on the revival of the team.
The preseason slate is done after Thursday’s 18-12 loss to the 49ers. Here’s an updated projection on who makes the final roster.
In: Kirk Cousins, Fernando Mendoza, Aidan O’Connell Out: Jacob Clark
Cousins and Mendoza are locked in as the team’s starter and backup, even if head coach Klint Kubiak won’t announce the order yet. All signs point to Cousins beginning the year as QB1.
The more interesting development among the Raiders’ quarterbacks is what happens with O’Connell. Kubiak and the staff like the fourth-year pro; they’ve praised him at every turn since their arrival. But O’Connell’s made it clear he wants to play, which he’s unlikely to do in Las Vegas. He’s also on the last year of his rookie contract. Las Vegas could trade him before Sunday, with a few teams in the market for backups. But O’Connell’s training camp and preseason play gives the Raiders reason to believe he’d competently lead them if Cousins isn’t available and Mendoza isn’t ready.
In: Ashton Jeanty, Mike Washington Jr., Dylan Laube, Dare Ogunbowale, Connor Heyward Out: Roman Hemby, Patrick Gurd
Jeanty’s injury weighs heavily on how the running back room shakes out. He suffered what is believed to be a sprained ankle in last Sunday’s practice; the team is hopeful he’ll avoid a long-term absence. If he’s ready for Week 1, it’s plausible that the Raiders roll with just him, Washington and Laube at tailback, and Heyward at fullback. If he’s out for the opener or longer, Las Vegas will have to keep more.
The Raiders added Ogunbowale late in training camp, and he had a few good plays against the Texans last week, including a 19-yard touchdown run. He’s been splitting reps with Laube on the second unit during practices since Jeanty went down. His performance, veteran experience and value on special teams give him a leg up over undrafted free agent Hemby. Las Vegas could explore the waiver market as well.
In: Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor, Jack Bech, Malik Benson, Dareke Young Injured Reserve: Donte Thornton Jr. Out: Deven Thompkins, Brandon Johnson, Shedrick Jackson, Phillip Dorsett II, Chase Roberts, E.J. Williams Jr.
While Kubiak has expressed dissatisfaction with his receiver group of late, the top four of Tucker, Nailor, Bech and rookie Benson seem to be locked in. Things get a little more murky after that.
Thornton, a 2025 fourth-round pick who started eight games as a rookie, missed the entire preseason with an undisclosed injury. He wasn’t necessarily flashing during training-camp practices while he was healthy. An Injured Reserve appointment with a designation to return seems likely if the Raiders want to further evaluate his place on the roster.
That leaves room for another receiver or two. Young seems to have a claim on a spot as a special-teams stalwart. Late signings Thompkins and Johnson also showed some offensive promise, but get left out in favor of depth elsewhere.
In: Brock Bowers, Michael Mayer, Ian Thomas Out: Carter Runyon, Albert Okwuegbunam Jr., Chris Myarick
Runyon’s unexplained absence since the first week of training camp makes this room pretty cut and dry. The second-year pro had a chance to push Thomas for the third tight end spot.
While only three guys will make up this group, tight end will be as important as it’s ever been for the Raiders. Las Vegas used heavy personnel sets at a rate that ranked in the top half of the league last season, and that will only increase under Kubiak. Bowers will be the engine that makes the offense go, while Mayer and Thomas should see significantly more opportunities than most second and third tight ends.
In: Kolton Miller, DJ Glaze, Tyler Linderbaum, Jackson Powers-Johnson, Spencer Burford, Caleb Rogers, Charles Grant, Trey Zuhn III Out: Jordan Meredith, Will Putnam, Dalton Wagner, Antonio Mafi, Braeden Daniels, Isaiah Jatta, Kamar Missouri, Niklas Henning
The Raiders’ starting offensive front is mostly settled, with Miller, Burford, Linderbaum and Glaze appearing to have locked in starting spots; it will be Powers-Johnson or Rogers at right guard. One of them will join tackle Grant and rookie utilityman Zuhn as important depth pieces.
Meredith, who started 11 games for the Raiders last year, appears to be a possible cut-day casualty after tumbling down the depth chart during the preseason. Las Vegas brought him back on a restricted free agent tender this offseason, but parting with him would cost them nothing and save money.
Las Vegas is counting on its three new additions (Linderbaum, Burford and Zuhn) and new offensive line coach Rick Dennison to buoy a unit that was the league’s worst last season. How well the group jells will have a massive effect on the capability of Kubiak’s under-center, run-focused offense.
In: Tonka Hemingway, Adam Butler, Jonah Laulu, Thomas Booker IV, Folorunso Fatukasi, JJ Pegues Out: Brandon Cleveland, Treven Ma’ae, Gary Smith III
Hemingway vaulted himself into a starting role after impressing in the spring. Butler, Laulu and Booker all mix in next to him when the Raiders deploy multiple interior linemen. Fatukasi, despite just being signed on Aug. 15, has impressed and carved out a role for himself as an early-down defender. Pegues, a 2025 sixth-round pick, should round out the group over rookies Cleveland and Smith, who are practice-squad candidates.
However, this group may be the biggest question mark for Las Vegas after a lackluster showing in the preseason. Opposing teams ran up the gut at will in each of the three games, with the second level having to clean up for some interior deficiencies. Fatukasi looks to be the best run stopper.
In: Maxx Crosby, Kwity Paye, Malcolm Koonce, Cian Slone, Patrick Johnson Injured Reserve: Keyron Crawford Out: Jahfari Harvey
The top four of this group looked rock solid until Thursday night when Crawford was carted off with an ankle injury. Kubiak didn’t offer any timeline for the third-round rookie, saying only that the team will “evaluate him further.” But a potential serious injury this close to cut-down day puts him in strong territory for an IR spot.
If Crawford does indeed require a designation, it eases one of the tougher decisions the Raiders would have had to face. Both Slone and Johnson have had strong training camps and preseasons, but six edges might have been too many to carry. An extra spot allows Las Vegas to reward both of the unheralded additions for their efforts.
In: Quay Walker, Nakobe Dean, Cody Lindenberg, Tommy Eichenberg, Segun Olubi Out: Cameron McGrone, Xavian Sorey Jr., Buddy Johnson
With the interior defensive line suspect, the linebacker group will be counted on heavily this season. Walker and Dean, two significant free-agent additions, have looked the part. On the starting defense’s two drives in the preseason finale, that pair was key in forcing a three-and-out on the first possession, and both made plays to shut down the second drive in five plays.
Questions come beyond that duo. Eichenberg and Lindenberg are the primary backups, and while the Raiders have expressed confidence in both, there’s a significant talent drop-off from the starters. Olubi, their one spring free-agent addition at the position, will be a key special-teams figure but not a defensive factor.
In: Eric Stokes, Darien Porter, Jermod McCoy, Hezekiah Masses, Decamerion Richardson Out: Greedy Vance, Caleb Offord, Devyn Perkins
Porter seems to have won the starting job opposite Stokes. The Raiders gave him all the first-team reps over the last week of practice, and sat him following the first two…
