full_text:
Patriots receiver Kyle Williams caught a touchdown pass for the third straight preseason game on Thursday, hauling in a 45-yard score from Tommy DeVito. Jason Miller / Getty Images
It’s good for the New England Patriots that Thursday night’s preseason finale didn’t matter. The defense was throttled in the first half, the offense struggled to run the ball once again and depth looks like a serious issue. They lost to the Browns 37-13 .
But now, the Pats turn the page to the regular season. The opener is less than two weeks away. And the initial 53-man roster is due Sunday evening.
With no more preseason games or practices before cutdown day, here’s our final attempt at predicting the Patriots’ opening roster.
In: Drake Maye, Tommy DeVito, Behren Morton
DeVito had a good training camp and looks like a capable backup, but everyone knows this is Maye’s show. A little regression after an incredible 2025 campaign would be understandable. But with an improved offensive line, better wide receivers and a second season in coordinator Josh McDaniels’ system, the sky is the limit for Maye.
In: Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson, Reggie Gilliam
Out: Lan Larison, Jam Miller, Hassan Haskins, JaMycal Hasty
It would be unconventional to keep just two running backs and a fullback. But hear me out: No running back separated himself from the others in the RB3 competition. Rather than hand the job to someone, why not stick two running backs (like Larison and Miller) on the practice squad? They can elevate a player from the practice squad twice before having to activate them, so that could buy the Patriots a month before having to make a decision on their No. 3.
In: A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, Mack Hollins, DeMario Douglas, Kyle Williams, Efton Chism
Out: Kyle Dixon, Nick DeGennaro, Cameron Dorner, Tejhaun Palmer
There’s much more clarity here after the trade of Kayshon Boutte . And after the deal, it was a great sign to see Williams have another strong preseason game. For the second straight contest, he beat a corner for a deep ball downfield, scoring a 45-yard touchdown against the Browns. He might just be a one-trick wide receiver, but he’s good at that one trick.
In: Hunter Henry, Eli Raridon, Tanner Arkin
Out: Jack Westover, CJ Dippre
It’s going to be interesting to see how McDaniels utilizes his tight ends. Raridon still needs to add strength, but he’s being thrust into the No. 2 job after an injury to Julian Hill. Does that mean McDaniels uses two-tight-end formations less than expected?
As for the No. 3 job, Arkin seems the likely winner as the true blocking tight end. But it wouldn’t be a shock if the Pats searched the waiver wire Saturday night for a blocking tight end with more experience.
In: Will Campbell, Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, Mike Onwenu, Morgan Moses, Caleb Lomu, Marcus Bryant, Dametrious Crownover, Greg Van Roten, James Hudson III
Out: Mehki Butler, Lorenz Metz, Jacob Rizy, JonDarius Morgan, Darrian Dalcourt, Joe Michalski, Jack Conley
The depth here is a bit of a mess. The Patriots signed Van Roten to be their catch-all interior offensive line backup, and they are putting a lot of stock into him picking up the offense and getting in football shape in a few short weeks.
Beyond that, the big question is whether Lomu or Bryant would be the first tackle off the bench to replace an injured player or in jumbo packages. Bryant was better in training camp, but Lomu was a first-round pick and thus comes with much more promise.
In: Dre’Mont Jones, Milton Williams, Christian Barmore, Gabe Jacas, Elijah Ponder, Cory Durden, Joshua Farmer, Eric Gregory, Quintayvious Hutchins, Bradyn Swinson
Out: Leonard Taylor III, Jeremiah Pharms Jr., Jesse Luketa, Xavier Holmes, Isaiah Iton, Casey Rogers
Injured: Harold Landry III
This is another spot where the Patriots lack depth, and it seems likely they’ll put in at least one waiver claim for someone to help on the D-line. The edge depth is a mess with Landry looking like he’ll miss Week 1. Jacas has good traits, but when he misses, he misses big — as we saw Thursday night. And the interior D-line lacks a true run stuffer, which contributed to their problems in that area throughout training camp.
In: Robert Spillane, Christian Elliss, K.J. Britt, Namdi Obiazor, Chad Muma
Out: Amari Gainer, Riley Wilson, Khalil Jacobs
Stop me if you’ve heard this before, but the Patriots lack depth here as well. Obiazor and Muma make the roster in this projection because, well, you need some linebackers to make it. It’s an important position for special teams.
The drawback for the Patriots entering the weekend? They have the 31st priority on waiver claims (out of 32 teams), which could hurt their ability to land reinforcements.
In: Christian Gonzalez, Carlton Davis III, Marcus Jones, Kindle Vildor, Charles Woods, Karon Prunty
Out: Kobee Minor, Marcellas Dial Jr., Brandon Crossley, Channing Canada
Thursday wasn’t a banner night for the backup cornerbacks, who watched as Dillon Gabriel dusted them for three touchdowns in the first half. Vildor had a nice second preseason game, Woods has plenty of experience and Prunty had some nice moments in training camp. You could make an argument for Canada here, too. But the lack of depth also underscores the importance of getting a deal done with Gonzalez.
In: Kevin Byard, Craig Woodson, Jaylen Reed, Dell Pettus
Out: John Saunders Jr., Mike Brown, Peter Manuma, Eric Butler
The Patriots tried signing some veteran safeties to add depth this spring, but they didn’t really work out, leading to the trade that landed them Reed. The Patriots don’t just think Reed can be a backup this season, but they expect him to be a core piece on special teams. And if things go well, he could factor into the starting competition next year for the job next to Woodson, since Byard is on a one-year deal.
In: Andy Borregales, Bryce Baringer, Julian Ashby
Haack punted well against the Browns, and it’s not really clear how serious Baringer’s injury is. Haack is probably the guy if Baringer isn’t ready for Week 1.

full_text:
Giants coach John Harbaugh has conducted 12 practice sessions lasting more than two hours. Just four of former coach Brian Daboll’s practices ran over two hours last year. Ben Queen / Imagn Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Friday’s NFL preseason action.
New York Giants coach John Harbaugh vowed at his introductory news conference that “we’re going to be doing football, all the time, every day.” As Harbaugh’s first training camp concludes with Friday’s preseason finale against the Jets, the veteran coach has kept his word.
The Giants have held 21 practices from the start of training camp to this point. They held 15 practices over the same stretch last year.
The difference comes from former coach Brian Daboll’s more frequent off days. Daboll never practiced more than three days in a row, and he gave two days off from practice after a preseason game. The Giants practiced on 10 of their 11 days in West Virginia to open camp this year, including six straight practices in the second week. Harbaugh has had the team back on the practice field after one day off following each preseason game.
Harbaugh’s practices have been longer, with 12 sessions lasting more than two hours. Just four of Daboll’s practices ran over two hours last year.
The early returns on the demanding schedule are promising, as the Giants dominated a joint practice against the lowly Dolphins in the oppressive Miami heat last week. The Giants almost made it through the grueling camp without incurring a major injury before wide receiver Calvin Austin suffered a non-contact torn ACL during a drill on Tuesday.
Harbaugh’s program got off to an inauspicious start when three players, including receiver/return Gunner Olszewski and defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris, suffered torn Achilles tendons during OTAs. But those were the only major injuries until the Giants lost Austin, who was slated to be the starting slot receiver.
It’s been notable how the Giants have avoided extended absences due to soft-tissue injuries. Even when players are injured, they seem to be returning to practice faster than past years. Assistant general manager Brandon Brown attributed the short stays on the sideline to the meritocracy Harbaugh has established.
“Guys don’t want to miss practice because they understand the floor is being raised and you missing practice is an opportunity, frankly, for someone else to take your job, and you see it in real time,” Brown said. “It’s not just lip service. You’ve seen rotations of players getting reps with the ones, now getting reps with the twos, guys that were fringed twos now getting reps with the ones.”
It’s not as if Harbaugh is running the players into the ground with no consideration for their bodies. Two of the camp practices were conducted at a jog-through pace to limit the physical demands while maintaining the mental intensity.
Every coach drills situational football, but Harbaugh dedicates more time to game management — leading late, trailing late, end of half, etc. — than any of the previous four Giants coaches I’ve covered in the post-Tom Coughlin era. No stone has gone unturned by Harbaugh. The Giants have rehearsed everything from their pregame stretching routine to the victory formation. It will be shocking if the Giants aren’t effective at converting on fourth-and-1 because they’ve seemingly drilled that situation as much as any other this summer.
Soon the Giants will find out if the more intense training camp translates to the regular season. They have dropped their past three openers by a combined score of 89-12.
The worth of training camp stats can be debated, but there’s value in having a tally of how many passes a receiver caught and from which quarterback.
Tight end Isaiah Likely was far and away starting quarterback Jaxson Dart’s favorite target with 44 catches in 11-on-11 team periods during camp. Wide receiver Darnell Mooney finished a distant second with 18 catches from Dart. Austin (17), TE Theo Johnson (17), WR Malachi Fields (15), RB Tyrone Tracy Jr. (14), RB Devin Singletary (13) and RB Cam Skattebo (12) were the other players with at least 10 catches from Dart in camp.
Dart completed 188-of-276 attempts (68.1 percent) in 11-on-11 periods with seven interceptions. Oddly, defensive tackle Darius Alexander was the only player with multiple interceptions of Dart this summer. For perspective on how much heavier Dart’s workload was as the starter this summer compared to the backup as a rookie, he completed 85-of-136 attempts (62.5 percent) in camp last year.
Backup quarterback Jameis Winston completed 156-of-244 passes (63.9 percent) in 11-on-11 periods. His favorite targets were TE Tanner Conner (16 catches), WR Dalen Cambre (16), WR Braxton Berrios (14), WR Xavier Gipson (13), RB Eric Gray (13) and TE Thomas Fidone (12).
Overall, the Giants’ quarterbacks attempted 617 passes in 11-on-11 periods this summer compared to 463 attempts last year under Daboll.
Harbaugh’s run of having an undrafted rookie make the roster — it happened 17 times in his 18 years in Baltimore — should continue with kicker Dominic Zvada. A three-man competition was quickly whittled down to two in the spring after the Giants determined veteran Jason Sanders didn’t have the leg strength necessary to kick in the Meadowlands (Sanders ironically went on to win the Jets’ kicking job).
That left Zvada against Ben Sauls, who went 8-for-8 on field goals in the final three games of last season as a rookie. Zvada was the clear leader in the competition after Sauls struggled badly in the spring, and the rookie never ceded his hold on the job.
Both kickers were perfect on kicks in the first two preseason games, but Zvada held a significant edge in practice. He made 81-of-90 field goals (90 percent) in live periods compared to 67-of-87 (77 percent) for Sauls. Both kickers have strong legs, as evidenced by makes from 60-plus yards in the last practice of camp, but Zvada’s booming power raises excitement over the possibility of the Giants having a weapon like the one the Cowboys discovered in Brandon Aubrey.
Special teams are a major consideration when forming a roster, and that is certainly the case under Harbaugh, who has an extensive special teams background. Insider linebackers Micah McFadden, Jack Kelly and Zaire Barnes, as well as outside linebacker Caleb Murphy and safety Elijah Campbell, have gotten extensive work as starters on the core four special teams units (kickoff, kickoff return, punt, punt return).
McFadden and Kelly are locks to make the roster as the backup inside linebackers. Barnes, Murphy and Campbell are unheralded players who are in prime position to make the roster because of their special teams value.
Gunner is an important position on the punt team. Campbell is in line for one of the gunner jobs, while the other position is up for grabs. Cornerback Art Green has been a standout gunner, but he has lost first-team reps on special teams recently. Nic Jones, who adds value as a backup slot corner, could swipe Green’s spot as a gunner.
Berrios appears to be a lock to make the roster as the punt returner after Austin’s injury. Berrios can also return kickoffs alongside Deonte Banks. None of the other wide receivers contribute on special teams, so that might mean whoever is lower on the depth chart between Darius Slayton and Odell Beckham Jr. will be inactive on game days.
It’s trending toward the Giants carrying four running backs on the active roster: Skattebo, Singletary, Tracy and Najee Harris. None of those backs have much special teams experience beyond some kick returns for Singletary and Tracy. Like at wide receiver, it will be challenging to dress all of the running backs on game day if they don’t contribute on special teams. Tracy is an option to return kickoffs alongside Banks, and he has been a starter on the punt team throughout the summer, so that could be his ticket to a jersey on game day.
Harbaugh favors a leadership group instead of traditional…

Dave Helman on what excites him most about the Eagles: A defense that I am certain is going to be very good and has at least the chance to be the very best in football. Every time I get nervous about the Jonathan Greenard situation and the fact that he hasn’t had a training camp, I just think about the defensive tackles the Eagles have available to them. And then you look at the depth chart on the edge, it may not be spectacular outside of Greenard, but they’re just so deep.
Derrik Klassen on what he’s watching the first month of the season: How do Jalen Hurts and, to a slightly different extent, the offensive line take to a new offense? It’s going to be a little bit more under center. They’re going to try to hit some of this play-action stuff a little bit more. And they’ve flirted with some of that stuff, I think, over the past couple of years, but it’s never felt like it was the core principle of the offense.
I just have questions about how comfortable Hurts is going to look in that. And then the offensive line, this is a lot of new for them, too. For as great as they’ve been, it’s also been very specific for them. It’s been a lot of the same gun, RPO, downhill type of stuff. And so the fact that that’s gonna be a little bit of a change for them, I just wonder if this is a thing where they look like they’re kind of ready to go out of the gate, or is this something that is more of an, ‘Okay, let’s see how it looks by Halloween and maybe we’re trying to figure out what concepts we like’ and that sort of thing.
Robert Mays on what’s keeping him up at night: Will the passing game be good enough? That’s where I sit with it. Joe Flacco and Cam Ward were the only quarterbacks in the NFL who had a worse success rate versus zone coverage last year than Jalen Hurts. I just wonder if the other stuff is diminished, if the offensive line is a step worse, if the running game is a step worse, if we don’t have A.J. Brown here anymore, if Makai Lemon comes along slowly, if Dontayvion Wicks doesn’t turn into that number two receiver that you feel excited about early in the season, is it good enough?
And I just don’t know. I think that there’s an argument that the under center stuff will unlock him in a way that he hasn’t been unlocked before, in part because it streamlines the decision making. Under center is the purest form of pure progression football. You’re not making a decision based on coverages where your gears are turning in real time. You’re turning around, whoever’s open, you’re throwing the ball to him. I actually think that that style of offense can coax something out of him that we really haven’t seen. We saw it in flashes last year. I’m open to that.
But what’s keeping me up at night is that this has been a plus 48 percent passing success rate team once since he’s been there, and the circumstances around him have deteriorated since then. And so you can make an argument that the scheme is more conducive to success, but that is still a question. This is a first-time play caller we’ve never seen do this before that has been coaching for two years. So is that path there? Yes. They could absolutely go down that one. But they could also go down the other one where every single aspect of this is not as good as it was when this offense and passing game felt Super Bowl caliber.

full_text:
Quarterback Jalen Hurts has spent most of Eagles training camp without his top receivers, who have dealt with injuries. Michael Owens / Getty Images
The Athletic has live coverage of Friday’s NFL preseason action.
Training camp is over. Well, at least its practices are. The Philadelphia Eagles host their preseason finale Friday against the Cincinnati Bengals.
It is the final opportunity for fringe players to secure a spot before the Eagles cut their roster to 53 players by Sunday’s 6 p.m. ET deadline.
The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena answered six pressing questions surrounding the Eagles, once again.
Berman: By letter grade, I’ll give him a B/B-. He practiced three weeks without DeVonta Smith and Makai Lemon, and any quarterback would look better with Smith. Hurts adjusted to the offense and embraced changes to footwork, cadence, operating under center, and throwing across the middle. Hurts calls it “sponge mode” this time of year. There’s something to be said about his willingness to embrace change at this point in his career. He made several high-level passes that Super Bowl MVPs and franchise quarterbacks make. But there were more inconsistencies than in previous summers, with inefficient practice. There were also far more interceptions. We’ll see what translates to games. I’ve also been impressed by his mobility and am curious how that factors into the offense this season. He’s had better camps in the past with A.J. Brown and Smith on the field. But Brown’s not here this season, so that point is moot. The key is keeping Smith (and Lemon) healthy. I’d be concerned about the passing game without him.
Kubena: I’ll also grade it a B. The uptick in interceptions is a red flag. Hurts was figuring out what works and what doesn’t in a very new system. Expecting Hurts to fully understand offensive coordinator Sean Mannion’s offense at this point is impractical. I expect he’s identified which risks he’s willing to take in the passing game in regular-season games, but that still leaves the question about what his alternatives are. He looks sound in his command of the pre-snap operation and in his technique under center. We never got the chance to consistently see whether the passing game can move the chains with Smith and Lemon on the field. My grade would have been a C after the first day of joint practices against the New England Patriots. But Hurts started finding a rhythm with his depth receivers thereafter. Tuesday’s practice at Lincoln Financial Field showcased the passing game’s ceiling. With another week of practices, I think my grade could have been an A.
Berman: Jalyx Hunt. He’s been terrific all summer. If you didn’t know the context and just watched practice, you would think he might be the best player on the team. Hunt was a menace rushing the quarterback. He was active in pursuit. He even had a highlight-reel interception in the joint practices against New England. I’m reluctant to call it a “breakout” season because the breakout might have already occurred — he led the team in sacks and interceptions last season — but he can reach an entirely different level in Year 3. The Eagles acquired Jonathan Greenard to be the No. 1 edge rusher. It’s no knock on Greenard, but we might be talking about Hunt as a front-line player and one of the top edge rushers in the NFL by the end of the season.
Kubena: Willie Lampkin. Your story about him on Wednesday detailed how he stole the spotlight within a veteran-laden offensive line this summer. Lampkin, a young and undersized player, transfused the Eagles with fresh blood. His dominant play at the depths of the lineup is the sort of thing that permeates the roster — and can create urgency from everyone. He may not start in a single game this season. But the value Lampkin created for himself by pushing his teammates all summer qualifies him for the sort of player I define as a training camp MVP.
Berman: Not necessarily. I entered training camp believing the defense would be one of the NFL’s best and the offense was still figuring itself out, and camp finished with the same sentiment. The injuries to wide receivers affected how I viewed the offense this summer, and I’ll give them the benefit of the doubt that Smith’s return will help. But I would not expect a prolific passing game. The key is the running game. I’ve been impressed with the way Saquon Barkley looks this summer, and the offense is built around a marriage between the run and the pass. If they can have one of the league’s most effective ground attacks, the passing game will improve. If not, the growing pains might feel more like persistent pains. I’m sold on this defense. They have blue-chippers at all three levels. They could have three to six All-Pros with one of the best coordinators in recent NFL history. This summer fortified that notion. (Also, the offense will benefit from not seeing Vic Fangio’s defense every day…)
Kubena: Yes. When head coaches talk about culture in press conference settings, there will generally be a question about how true that actually is. Nick Sirianni emphasized closeness over the summer. He talked about how tight-knit the New York Knicks and the San Antonio Spurs were and how the best teams he’s had in Philadelphia were the closest ones. The Eagles were observably close in training camp. It isn’t so much that this changed the way I viewed the season. I just needed to see it for myself. Players routinely popped into scrums to support their teammates. A.J. Epenesa credited the encouragement he’s received in the edge rusher group as “what’s been helping propel me forward” as he learns a new position.
Sure, Moro Ojomo and Fred Johnson went two rounds on back-to-back plays a few weeks ago, but Ojomo owned up to it and apologized afterward. The signs were there that these Eagles can be a tight-knit group. Some pundits will cite Brown’s absence. Indeed, Brown’s misery in 2025 was the most outward expression of an offensive system that frustrated everyone. If schematic bugs and other problems arrive for the Eagles to solve in 2026, misery seems less likely.
Berman: We’ve discussed backup quarterback throughout the summer, and there hasn’t been a clear runaway winner in that competition. The Eagles are deep at inside linebacker, and general manager Howie Roseman could have a difficult decision to make figuring out the last one to keep. The Uar Bernard and Joshua Weru decisions are complicated because neither player is likely to contribute this year. Still, the potential might be too great to expose either to waivers and risk another team making the investment. One point readers should keep in mind over the next 48 hours: Roseman isn’t putting a 53-man roster together; he’s viewing it as a 70-man roster, including the practice squad and one additional player for the IPP spot. There’s a level of strategy to final cutdowns that goes beyond, “keep the 53 best players.”
Kubena: In terms of starters, the Eagles have one of the best secondaries in the NFL. There is a significant drop-off in its depth. What they do there will affect whether they have room for Bernard and/or Weru. Will they choose to carry just three safeties knowing Cooper DeJean is essentially a fourth? And who is their best backup option at outside cornerback behind Quinyon Mitchell and Riq Woolen? Mac McWilliams and Kelee Ringo have had a spotty training camp. Jonathan Jones and Jakorian Bennett spent most of the summer on the sideline with injuries. Ambry Thomas and Isaiah Bolden were both burned for touchdowns against the Patriots. DeJean can’t be the emergency option for every position — can he?
Berman: I’m focusing on tight end and safety. If the Eagles are going to play more heavy packages, they need the tight ends to worry defenses. It’s not enough to say you’ll play 12 personnel — it needs to force the defense to figure out what personnel groups they’ll match it with and to be able to exploit mismatches. Eli Stowers’ quiet summer makes it…

full_text:
Tatum Bethune, center, started eight games last season and had an interception against the Raiders on Thursday night, but his roster spot is not assured. Ian Maule / Getty Images
LAS VEGAS — Sometimes scores can be misleading. The San Francisco 49ers and Las Vegas Raiders’ tie at 12 at the two-minute warning in Thursday night’s preseason finale was not.
Eddy Piñeiro, who made a 59-yard attempt earlier, kicked a 51-yard field goal for the lead and a 54-yarder as insurance, giving him six field goals in the 18-12 win, but the 49ers were already content to walk away from the boring affair with only one more injured 53-man-roster player than they had coming in: rookie cornerback Ephesians Prysock, who left in the first quarter with a sprained shoulder.
There wasn’t much to be gained in the preseason finale, as only a couple of the 49ers’ potential starters played against the Raiders.
Keion White used a swim move for a sack and was all over the field in a good test, as the Raiders played their offensive starters. Fourth-round rookie Carver Willis , who might be the opening-day starter at left guard by default, was up and down like the rest of the offensive line. The 49ers ran for 91 yards on 15 carries in the first half, but the line did get stuffed twice in short yardage, and the passing game never got going, as Mac Jones and Adrian Martinez combined for 137 yards passing (only 42 yards in the first half).
Niners coach Kyle Shanahan smiled when asked whether any players stood out to him.
“ Um, I mean, yeah, there are a few guys,” he said. “I have no problem with praising people, but people in this league get paid a lot of money to read everything we say and evaluate decisions over these next three days based off of practice squads and depth charts and stuff. So I got to be pretty careful with that.”
With the preseason complete, we’ve tag-teamed the final projection for the 49ers’ roster ahead of Sunday’s 3 p.m. PT cutdown deadline, with Vic Tafur handling the offense and Matt Barrows the defense.
Notes: The projection includes three players going to injured reserve with a designation to return (and mentions others who could be IR candidates). Only two players can be given that designation before the cutdown deadline, which could mean additional transactions Monday. Rookies in italics.
Injured reserve: Kurtis Rourke
Rourke has three broken ribs, which actually gives the 49ers some flexibility, as they would have had to carry three quarterbacks on the roster to keep him, the potential backup in 2027 if Jones leaves to pursue a starting job next offseason. Putting him on short-term IR would rule him out for at least four weeks without taking up a roster spot.
Jones has been a little erratic this preseason and training camp, but he was great last season, winning five of eight starts, and a case could be made the 49ers have the best quarterbacks group in the NFL.
Barrows’ counterpoint: This scenario would leave the 49ers with only two quarterbacks available early on, unless they got Martinez on the practice squad and elevate him for games. That’s certainly possible, though they can elevate only two players per week and might need to use those spots elsewhere. Also, they can elevate Martinez only three times before he would have to be signed to the 53-man roster to be eligible for another game.
Cut: Sincere McCormick, Khalil Herbert
The top three running backs all missed time during training camp, but they’re all ramping up and look very good. James had a 20-yard catch-and-run on a screen and a 17-yard bulldozing run Thursday night. Black, who had a 14-yard run, returned to camp before James and seems to have a firm hold on the No. 2 job, thanks to how hard he hits the hole, good vision and underrated hands.
Injured reserve: Christian Kirk
Cut: KhaDarel Hodge, Will Pauling , Wesley Grimes , Malik Turner, Trenton Irwin
Cowing was firmly on the bubble until that touchdown on a punt return last week, and he should send some steaks to the Los Angeles Chargers’ punter. If JK Scott made any kind of effort to tackle Cowing, it would have been a ho-hum 30-yard return for an injury-plagued receiver. Cowing is now battling a groin injury.
Kirk’s calf injury on the first day of camp lingered, and if he goes on IR, that would give Cowing and Watkins — who had four catches for 64 yards and three carries for 19 yards Thursday night — at least another four weeks to make an impression. Robinson seems to have moved past those two because of Purdy’s trust in the vet.
Cut: Brayden Willis, Khalil Dinkins , Hayden Rucci
Worst-case scenario, Kittle will be back from his Achilles injury for Week 2 and a three-game homestand. Best case, he’ll give the Los Angeles Rams something to worry about in Australia. The 49ers won’t rush him because they believe in Tonges — he scored the winning touchdown in the season opener in Seattle last year, and Shanahan said he has improved from last season. Willis turned some heads in early August, as he always does, but ran out of steam again.
Cut: Brandon Parker, Nick Zakelj, Drake Nugent, Isaac Alarcon, Doug Kramer Jr.
Shanahan said after the game Willis is making a strong push to win the left guard job, and the 49ers hope to have that decided when they return to practice Monday.
A quick tip of the cap to ninth-year vet Parker, who had a great day in one-on-ones in practice Tuesday and will likely be available for the 49ers’ practice squad again. He could even make the roster, as Lowe’s ankle injury is lingering a month later.
Why keep 11 O-linemen? Several are dealing with injuries (including Puni with lingering concussion issues), and the 49ers — a contending team — have to stand firm with the decision to hold a spot for a raw fifth-round rookie (Cruz) who is a year or two away from being ready to play in a regular-season game.
Barrows’ counterpoint: Lowe could begin the season on injured reserve, which would put Pleasants in the swing tackle role he had last year and free up another roster spot. Toth’s lingering concussion symptoms, meanwhile, create concern at backup center. If he can’t play in Australia — or make the 16-hour plane trip — the 49ers would have to think about having Nugent or Kramer in uniform in Week 1. Perhaps Nugent will land on the practice squad and get elevated against the Rams.
Cut: DT Sebastian Valdez, DT Bryson Eason, DT Evan Anderson, DE Ogbo Okoronkwo, DE Quinton Bell, DE Viliami Fehoko Jr., DE Jah Joyner
Thompson, an undrafted rookie, has arguably outplayed all the defensive linemen from this year’s rookie class and last year’s as well. He’s certainly been the healthiest. He, Eason and Valdez have been resilient since the spring, and the 49ers will try to get that group onto the active roster or practice squad.
The team also could stand to stash a defensive end — Okoronkwo? — on the practice squad and elevate him for games early on while Williams rounds into form. Starting the season on PUP means Williams must miss the first four games, but he could rejoin practice after two weeks.
Tafur’s counterpoint: I think the 49ers would be happy with any combination of Thompson, Eason and Valdez on the practice squad, which is why I think they’ll go with only eight D-linemen or with Okoronkwo as the ninth .
Cut: Tatum Bethune, Deion Jones, Larry Worth III , Jalen Graham
Gifford or Bethune? Yes, Bethune played well as the backup middle linebacker last year while Gifford — who had a concussion in the spring and a hamstring issue in the summer — has largely been absent. Still, Gifford made the Pro Bowl last year as a special teamer, and coordinator Brant Boyer will likely go to bat for him as cutdown day approaches. Wallow, meanwhile, might have displaced Bethune, despite his interception in Las Vegas on Thursday night, as the backup middle linebacker.
Not only will Dugger make the 53-man squad, but there’s a good chance he’ll start against the Rams on Sept. 10. He’s their best bet as the third linebacker — and tight end stopper…

full_text:
Brock Purdy, Christian McCaffrey and the Niners look to dethrone the Seattle Seahawks in 2026. Ezra Shaw / Getty Images
The San Francisco 49ers hit 2026 with a twinge of unique, specific longing. No other NFL franchise has been so consistently close to catharsis across the 21st century.
Since 2010, San Francisco has endured three tough Super Bowl losses and four others in the NFC Championship Game. But the 2026 roster is certainly talented enough to break through, even in the formidable NFC West.
Brock Purdy is under center as one of football’s steadier quarterbacks. Christian McCaffrey resumes his role as a three-down bellwether. While the tough-as-nails George Kittle recovers from an Achilles tear, Purdy’s other targets include perennial Pro Bowler Mike Evans, promising rookie De’Zhaun Stribling and the versatile Deebo Samuel Sr. in his return to the team.
On the other side, the defense is paced by all-world linebacker Fred Warner. New 49ers defensive coordinator Raheem Morris leads a high-upside group, so long as pass rushers Nick Bosa and Mykel Williams can bounce back from injuries.
Kyle Shanahan continues to prove himself as an innovative play caller. “ Bang Bang Niner Gang ” is always one of the loudest home crowds in American sports. The NFL’s schedule makers clearly consider San Francisco to be a must-see team, from its unprecedented Australian feature in Week 1 against the rival Los Angeles Rams, to a “Sunday Night Football” trip to Mexico City in Week 11 against the Minnesota Vikings.
Follow the team on The Athletic , and keep up with our beat reporters. Matt Barrows and Vic Tafur are Joe Montana and Steve Young with the pen.
All times listed below are ET.
The most expansive option for live game coverage is a multichannel plan. That includes streamers like Fubo, Sling TV and YouTube TV, or more traditional providers like DirecTV, Dish and Xfinity. We lay out cord-cutting alternatives for each NFL media partner down below, but there’s a certain peace of mind to the consolidation of pay television.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, AFC Championship Game
Each week, CBS carries games across two Sunday kickoff slots: one at 1 p.m., and another at 4:05 p.m. or the national window at 4:25 p.m. There will be 10 nationwide Sunday doubleheaders this year on CBS. Broadcasts are set by region when there are multiple offerings in a spot.
It’s not a clean split, but CBS is known as the primary home of the AFC. The network’s theme music is a certified slapper.
Its main pregame show, “The NFL Today,” adds recent retirees Russell Wilson and Kyle Long to its studio crew. CBS announcers include Jim Nantz and Ian Eagle, while the color commentary rotation stars JJ Watt.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an indoor TV antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local CBS games also stream on Paramount+.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (in-market fans)
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, NFC Championship Game
Like CBS, Fox splits Sunday afternoons between early 1 p.m. action and later 4:05/4:25 p.m. matchups. Its centerpiece is branded as “America’s Game of the Week.” Unlike CBS, Fox has a dancing robot named Cleatus . It’s the nominal network for the NFC as well.
Kevin Burkhardt, Joe Davis and Adam Amin are the lead play-by-play voices. Burkhardt pairs with Tom Brady, while Davis calls games alongside Greg Olsen. Amin is partnered with newcomer Drew Brees, who is fresh off his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction. Some Spanish-language broadcasts are available on Fox Deportes.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing. Local Fox games also stream on Fox One.
Main window: Sunday afternoon (out-of-market fans)
These two are the access points for all non-national matchups that aren’t on regional CBS or Fox.
NFL Sunday Ticket has full games. It’s exclusive to YouTube and YouTube TV. Those without a YouTube TV plan can still get NFL Sunday Ticket as a primetime channel through the standard YouTube app.
RedZone is the whip-around program that jumps around the slate to cover scoring drives. This is the place for Scott Hanson , “the witching hour” and chaotic octobox split screens. It can be added to NFL Sunday Ticket, and it’s included on some high-end pay TV sports plans.
RedZone also lives on NFL+ Premium, which can be bundled with the ESPN Unlimited plan.
What you’ll need to watch: An NFL Sunday Ticket subscription through YouTube TV or the YouTube app; NFL RedZone access through select pay TV packages, ESPN Unlimited or NFL+ Premium.
Playoffs: 2 wild-card games, 1 divisional game
This is the faithful home of “Sunday Night Football” each weekend. And because everything has to be confusing, the NBC lineup opens with a Wednesday night season premiere. At least SNF has a consistent 8:20 p.m. start time.
Mike Tirico and Cris Collinsworth are in the booth, with Melissa Stark reporting from the sidelines. Carrie Underwood sings about waiting all day for Sunday night . NBC’s “Football Night in America” pregame show brings on longtime head coach Mike Tomlin. Telemundo has the telecasts in Spanish.
The network has two extra Saturday offerings for Week 17. One is exclusive to Peacock, and both matchups will be announced later in the season. The same goes for NBC’s Week 18 regular-season finale.
“Sunday Night Football” is subject to flex scheduling — games can be swapped in and out of the window twice between Weeks 5-10 and any time from Weeks 11-17. This allows executives to pick games with greater playoff implications, though it leaves the actual ticket holders in a bind.
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for free over-the-air viewing, or a Peacock account with the live sports plan.
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game, 1 divisional game, Super Bowl LXI
The Disney networks combine to cover 17 “Monday Night Football” games. Ten of those are on both ABC and ESPN, with another seven exclusive to the latter. The oft-maligned “Monday Night Football” doubleheader is now a thing of the past.
MNF kickoffs have 8:15 p.m. starts, and their schedule flexes can happen any time in Weeks 12-17.  The two Saturday ABC/ESPN matchups in Week 18 will be set as the postseason picture sharpens.
ESPN is preparing for its first Super Bowl broadcast ever on Feb. 14, 2027. It will be simulcast on ABC.
Joe Buck handles play-by-play for MNF. He’s joined by analyst Troy Aikman, plus the sideline duo of Lisa Salters and Laura Rutledge. Spanish-language airings can be found on ESPN Deportes. For 12 regular-season games and the Super Bowl, ESPN2 offers an alternate “ManningCast,” in which Eli and Peyton Manning watch the games with famous fans. Guests have ranged from Bill Belichick to Lil Wayne .
What you’ll need to watch: A pay TV package, or an antenna for ABC, or an ESPN Unlimited account.
Main window: Thursday night
Playoffs: 1 wild-card game
Most weeks begin with “Thursday Night Football,” which kicks off at 8:15 p.m. Those games are behind the Prime paywall, but they’re free over the air in the participants’ home markets. Flex rules around TNF are a bit less hectic, with two allotments between Weeks 13-17.
Thursdays are called by Al Michaels and Kirk Herbstreit, with Kaylee Hartung on sideline duty. Herbstreit loves dogs ; Michaels hates vegetables . Prime has Spanish-language coverage and advanced stat broadcast options within its app. Former Niner Richard Sherman is one of the personalities for the pregame, halftime and postgame shows.
What you’ll need to watch: Amazon Prime. TNF is also free on Twitch with a registered account.
The league-owned media outlet is now under ESPN’s purview, thanks to a blockbuster deal that gave the NFL a 10 percent ownership stake in “The Worldwide Leader in Sports.” As of July 30, NFL Network is integrated into the ESPN Unlimited plan. It can also be accessed through NFL+ or NFL+ Premium.

“The Athletic Football Show” is previewing all 32 teams ahead of the 2026 NFL season. Below are select quotes from the show’s preview of the Washington Commanders. The quotes are edited for clarity. Dave Helman on what about the Commanders most excites him: Two years is an eternity in the NFL, but a healthy Jayden Daniels has proven he can make chicken salad out of chicken s— before. And he did it in 2024 without Laremy Tunsil, so the fact that Tunsil’s out for the year, it definitely sucks. But Jayden’s made do with less before. And I’m hoping he can stay healthy long enough to do it again. It’s an older duo than you would prefer, but Terry McLaurin and Stefon Diggs — if Diggs looks remotely like the guy from last year — I could talk myself into that.
Robert Mays on what he’s watching the first month of the season: I’m curious what David Blough is going to get from this offense that Kliff Kingsbury couldn’t. If you look at the numbers, Kliff was middle of the pack last year with Jayden missing a huge chunk of the season. And they were really good in ’24. Kliff Kingsbury did a really good job as the offensive coordinator for the Commanders. The argument is: Can we be harder to play against?
Every run concept is on the table if we’re under center. If we’re using more play action, if we’re doing all these different things, can we just be harder to play against? I think that is the goal on both sides of the ball. On defense, you can get me there pretty easily. On offense, it’s one of those be-careful-what-you-wish-for sort of things.
Derrik Klassen on what’s keeping him up at night: What if it just doesn’t really all make sense together, and what if the offensive line is not able to do some of the stuff they want to do? What if they don’t really have the personnel to do some of the stuff they want to do? It still, to me, feels like a personnel group that should be more gun and spread.
When Stefon Diggs and Terry McLaurin are your two best receivers, and the guy you draft is like a slot only, you should be a little bit more gun open. Chig Okonkwo being your leading tight end, you should be a little bit more spread and gun open. Your running backs being Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Rachaad White — you should have the flexibility of having him in gun where he can be out in the route or out in protection for you a little bit easier. I wonder how they make that work with what is supposed to be a more under-center approach.

title: Three Bold Predictions for Cardinals vs Packers Preseason Finale
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers are hoping to put on a show to finish preseason festivities.
60 minutes of action at Lambeau Field is the only thing standing in the way of an important weekend for both teams, where the Cardinals and Packers will cut their rosters down to 53 ahead of the regular season.
Starters aren't expected to play tonight, opening the door for just about anything to happen with backups taking the field.
Three bold predictions for tonight:
The bottom of the Cardinals' WR room is in a tight race to compete for a potential WR6 spot in the desert with Jalen Brooks and Ihmir Smith-Marsette leading the way.
Brooks has recently gained momentum with strong outings in preseason games. Smith-Marsette had the early lead thanks to work with the Cardinals' starters on offense and special teams.
Both need to put a cherry on top of their work before roster cuts arrive Sunday, and that's not lost on either player. The good news? Arizona's offense has (mostly) been humming and players are capable of finding the end zone.
There's no Jacoby Brissett or Carson Beck tonight, paving the way for Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis to play snaps under center.
In fairness, all four quarterbacks have seen success running Mike LaFleur's offense. However, both Minshew and Slovis are prone to making mistakes — especially against an aggressive Jonathan Gannon-led defense (more on him in a minute).
Minshew's style of play is exactly that of a gun-slinger, a passer who isn't afraid to take chances. While that can lead to some exciting moments, that also places the ball in danger of heading the other way.
As for Slovis, he went just 2/7 passing against the Cowboys last weekend. He's staring down what is very likely his last bit of playing time for 2026, and he'll likely look to go down swinging before he's sent to waivers.
Who doesn't love a good revenge game?
Gannon was fired by the Cardinals this past offseason and now looks to rebound with the Super Bowl-ready Packers. There's a plethora of talent on both sides of the ball, including Micah Parsons returning at some point under Gannon.
Realistically, Gannon's not going to reveal exotic stuff tonight against his former team. It wouldn't be worth exposing film for the regular season.
Calling it bad blood between the two sides just might even be a stretch.
Still, Gannon likes to have a good time — and that just might include dialing up a bit more pressure than usual against a backup Cardinals OL that lost Chase Bisontis earlier in the preseason.

title: Cardinals vs. Packers: 2 Best Bets for Tonight's Preseason Finale
full_text:
It's nearly time for the Arizona Cardinals and Green Bay Packers to square off at Lambeau Field for tonight's preseason finale for both sides.
With starters not expected to play , fans of Arizona and Green Bay are sure to see a handful of position battles finalize while players can make or break their chances of landing on the final roster.
Case in point, there's still plenty riding on tonight's game for both sides — and it should be plenty entertaining.
If you're looking for action tonight, here's two of the best bets we found on the internet:
Iain MacMillan, SI.com: "Instead of betting on a side in this game, I'm going to bet the OVER in the LaFleur Bowl. Both offenses have been strong so far in the postseason. The Cardinals have hung 30+ points in two of their three games, and the Packers are coming off a 33-point performance against the Broncos, who have one of the best defenses in the NFL.
"Quarterbacks for both teams have also been impressive thus far. Gardner Minshew has been great for the Cardinals, and Carson Beck is on track to get back on the field. The 2025 sixth-round pick Kyle McCord has also been good for the Packers. More often than not, good quarterback play is all a game needs to hit the OVER in a preseason affair.
"Let's sit back and root for points in this one."
Our take: We're not sure where MacMillan is getting his information, as Beck hasn't thrown a pass in practice in roughly two weeks and would be a massive surprise to play tonight. Though the Cardinals haven't officially ruled him out (since they're in Green Bay and not meeting with local reporters) the overwhelming expectation is Beck won't play.
Michael Crosson, Action Network: "In the chaotic preseason environment, public perception routinely overreacts to single-week scoring margins. By taking the moneyline on overlooked underdogs in tight-spread settings, bettors capitalize on market mispricings driven by public bias than actual on-field execution.
"... Our internal tracking shows early public action heavily skewed toward Green Bay, drawing 76% of bets and 93% of total money. In reality, the wrong team is likely favored here. Arizona possesses the superior backup quarterback tandem in Minshew and Slovis, an offense averaging over 240 passing yards per game through three preseason games, and the LaFleur brother who seems to have more personal incentive to compete.
"We'll fade the public overreaction and back the Cardinals on the moneyline."
Our take: Moneyline bets always feel like a toss-up in preseason, and with practically no starters playing in this game, it truly does feel like a coin-flip. What we can say about Arizona's offense is it hasn't mattered who operates it — it's looked fairly solid. With that said, Slovis didn't look exactly strong against the Dallas Cowboys last week.

title: How to Watch Cardinals' Preseason Finale vs. Packers (Start Time, Channel, Who to Monitor & More)
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals' preseason is nearly over.
Just 60 minutes of football at Lambeau Field separates the Cardinals from the regular season. Neither Arizona or the Packers are expected to field their starters tonight, though with roster cut day approaching on Sunday, this might just be the Cardinals' most important battle of the preseason.
It's one more opportunity for head coach Mike LaFleur and his staff to evaluate the roster ahead of some tough decisions looming this weekend. This is also the final time LaFleur will be able to see his offense in live action before the wins and losses begin to count.
Here's everything you need to know ahead of Friday's Cardinals vs. Packers preseason finale, including how to watch and one important position to monitor.
One of the Cardinals' biggest debates is how many receivers the team will carry on their final 53-man roster. Big names such as Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne are obvious choices while new additions in Devin Duvernay and fifth-round pick Reggie Virgil feel safe, too.
If Arizona does keep a sixth wideout, Brooks and Smith-Marsette feel like the top two candidates competing for the job.
Smith-Marsette initially had the lead in this race after an impressive training camp, which featured some rotation with the first-team Cardinals offense on top of special teams duties. He's considered the secondary returner after Duvernay.
However, Brooks has built some serious momentum in recent weeks thanks to his performance in preseason games — making plays deep down the field and being a reliable target for multiple Cardinals quarterbacks between the white lines.
There's a possibility neither is chosen on Arizona's roster ( matching our 53-man roster prediction) , though that doesn't make tonight any less interesting: teams around the league will be watching film from the game, effectively making this a try-out ahead of a busy weekend across the NFL.

title: Latest Jeremiyah Love Update is What Cardinals Fans Want to Hear
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals lost star rookie running back Jeremiyah Love to a high ankle injury during preseason play — one that's not only kept him out for the remainder of exhibition action but possibly the team's regular season opener as well.
Love, who hasn't practiced since departing Las Vegas with his injury, is reportedly making good progress and is trending in the right direction to be available for Arizona's Week 1 matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers.
"Jeremiyah Love trending in the right direction for week one needs to keep progressing though - still a ways to go but looking positive," Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro said of Love on a recent X post.
He also gave an update on Carson Beck — which you can read more about here .
Some Cardinals talk - Jeremiyah Love trending in the right direction for week one needs to keep progressing though - still a ways to go but looking positive. Carson Beck unlikely to start on IR - lost a chance at some valuable reps so that hurts we all were excited to see him…
Love tallied 14 total touches against the Raiders in what was likely his only glimpse of preseason action before LaFleur post-game described his ankle injury as something he likely could have returned with.
At the time, the Cardinals didn't seem worried about Love's injury. Love himself spoke with reporters in the locker room of Allegiant Stadium and seemed to be in good spirits.
Since the team returned from Vegas the injury seemingly regressed, and the Cardinals' running back room added another body to the sidelines with James Conner currently not playing/practicing and Trey Benson landing on injured reserve .
Love impressed in the short amount of time he played against the Raiders, stacking on top of an exciting training camp to generate legitimate buzz around the Valley.
He holds potential to be a game-changer for the Cardinals.
"He's doing well, progressing well, and kind of in the next phase of it," LaFleur said on Love earlier this week before confirming he wouldn't practice against the Packers.
Even as a rookie in a crowded backfield, Love figures to be a prominent part of Arizona's offense thanks to his ability to impact the rushing and receiving game at high levels.
“He really could come to our room if he ever wanted to,” Cardinals wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. said of Love. “Seeing him on twitch routes killing backers is laughable sometimes.”
Between his injury and Week 1 in Los Angeles, Love will have had nearly a calander month to recover and prepare to play against the Chargers. It's likely even if Love is active, the Cardinals may ease his workload thanks to Tyler Allgeier's presence in the room.

title: Cardinals Insider Sets Record Straight on Carson Beck, Injured Reserve Rumors
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals QB Carson Beck was supposed to get hefty run during preseason play as a third-round rookie, though that's yet to happen.
Beck, who suffered a ribs injury in the Hall of Fame Game, hasn't played in preseason action since and very likely isn't going to play in Green Bay for tonight's finale against the Packers. Not only has he been sidelined on gamedays, he also hasn't practiced in weeks.
That's led some to believe Beck could potentially be a candidate to land on injured reserve ahead of final roster cuts, which would see him miss the first four games of the 2026 regular season.
"I'm not going to dive into it because we don't have to worry about that right now," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said when asked about Beck playing in the regular season.
"When we get closer, I'll answer that for you."
However, Arizona Sports' John Gambadoro says that's Beck landing on injured reserve isn't likely to happen.
"Carson Beck unlikely to start on IR - lost a chance at some valuable reps so that hurts we all were excited to see him play more after what he did in the first preseason game," he wrote on X this week .
The Cardinals are unlikely to play Jacoby Brissett tonight in Lambeau Field, setting Gardner Minshew and Kedon Slovis up for playing time to conclude preseason festivities.
Beck impressed in the short time we saw him on the field, grading out as one of Pro Football Focus' top preseason quarterbacks while showing a little of everything that made him an enticing Day 2 pick in this past draft.
Beck won't be Arizona's starter to begin the regular season thanks to Brissett's presence, though there's a common belief the Cardinals could turn to the Miami product if Arizona's tough schedule ultimately gets the best of them in the win-loss column.

title: NFL Insider Reveals Truth on Josh Sweat Trade Rumors Involving Cardinals, Packers
full_text:
ARIZONA — Trade rumors continue to swirl around the Arizona Cardinals and Josh Sweat, though perhaps the biggest NFL insider just doused that chatter with his latest update.
Sweat, recently activated off the PUP list after managing a knee injury, traveled with the team to Green Bay with the Packers at the forefront of potential talks.
The Cardinals aren't trading Sweat at this moment. And if you don't want to take our word for it , you can take Adam Schefter's:
The prominent ESPN NFL insider appeared on ESPN Milwaukee to clear the air on any Sweat trade rumors:
"I try to deal in facts and realities. All I can tell you is I know there have been teams that have reached out to them [Arizona] and I know they've been told they're not trading him. Now, could they change their stance down the line? Sure, but there have been teams that recently have reached out and they've told those teams, 'We are not trading him.'"
"I know there have been teams that have reached out to them, and I know they've been told they're NOT trading him." #GoPackGo 🎙️ @AdamSchefter on whether the #Packers could trade for Josh Sweat. pic.twitter.com/IFBBQjTcan
Schefter isn't the only prominent NFL insider to debunk Sweat-to-Green Bay, as Ian Rapoport did so earlier in the offseason :
"This has gained some steam on social media, so just to provide some clarity: #AZCardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat is not being traded. Not to the #Packers or anywhere. Carry on…" he said on X.
This matches words from Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort earlier in camp, where he shut down any trade rumors :
Head coach Mike LaFleur, when speaking at minicamp while Sweat wasn't practicing, debunked any rumblings of a trade.
"There's no situation," LaFleur said.
"The situation is he hasn't practiced. I'm not going to put a guy out on the field that hasn't been out there to prep."
Sweat, after the Cardinals canned Jonathan Gannon to begin the offseason, reportedly requested a trade. That went unsettled through the offseason, and his absence through all of voluntary OTAs, minicamp and training camp didn't quite extinguish those talks.
Sweat had his two best statistical seasons under Gannon, who is believed to be a major driving point in landing Sweat via free agency. Gannon's absence mixed with Arizona's low expectations have contributed to some suspecting the star pass rusher isn't happy.
Sweat's practically their only prominent pass rusher. He led the Cardinals in sacks last season with 12 while every other rostered outside linebacker totaled just 5.5 combined. His pass rush win-rate also ranked near the top of the league.
Especially with Ossenfort's job potentially on the line this season, Arizona isn't exactly eager to offload one of their top players before the 2026 season even begins.
This could be a conversation later down the road, though for now, Sweat's not going anywhere.

title: Cardinals QB Update: What We Know About Who Will Play vs. Packers
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are set to play the Green Bay Packers in Friday's preseason finale, setting up one final opportunity for head coach Mike LaFleur and his staff to evaluate who can truly make a difference as roster cuts approach .
All eyes, per usual, are on the quarterback position for the Cardinals. Here's what we know about who is — and isn't — playing in Green Bay:
The Cardinals are not playing most of their starters this week in Green Bay, which would preclude Brissett from playing against the Packers on Friday. Brissett is the established QB1 to begin the season, though all eyes are paying careful attention to how the situation unfolds over the course of the season.
Drawing this back to present day, Brissett and the Cardinals' offense got off to a slow start during joint practice but quickly found their groove against Green Bay , especially at the end of practice.
Prediction: Brissett isn't dressed, alongside a vast majority of starters
Minshew is likely in line to play on Friday as Arizona's effective QB2. With Brissett not dressed, Minshew probably will get a drive or two before the Cardinals shelve him as well.
It's been a fun camp/preseason with Minshew under center, as his willingness to take chances downfield has led to some exciting plays. On the other side of the coin, Minshew is more prone to turnovers.
Early in the regular season, he very well could be the guy to take over if Brissett is forced out of action.
Prediction : Minshew will play a quarter of football before calling it a night at Lambeau Field.
Beck lit the preseason world on fire after his Hall of Fame Game outing, but he hasn't played since. The third-round pick reportedly picked up a ribs injury against Carolina and has been sidelined after trying to push through the pain.
Beck hasn't thrown in any practice over the last week and didn't participate in joint practice festivities against the Packers — which essentially makes him a longshot to play in a live-action game.
Prediction: Beck doesn't play as a precaution for his ribs injury.
We've arrived to the man of the hour.
Slovis is heavily favored to get majority of snaps under center for the Cardinals thanks to Brissett/Beck not playing and Minshew being a high level backup. With Arizona's quarterback room essentially settled, Slovis will be putting on tape for 31 other teams to evaluate this weekend.
The good news? Slovis has performed fairly well in LaFleur's offense this preseason, and that should again be the case.
Prediction: Slovis plays the final three quarters for Arizona, taking over for Minshew.

title: Cardinals Mailbag: Could Arizona Make a Surprise Move Before Week 1?
full_text:
ARIZONA — Just one preseason game stands in the way of the Arizona Cardinals and tough roster decisions.
The Cardinals, along with the rest of the league, are due to cut their roster down to 53 at 3:00 PM AZ time on Sunday – which will see almost half of their current players sent to waivers.
Thanks for all the questions, as always. Let's get into it:
This isn't completely out of the realm of possibility.
I'm not personally buying any of the Josh Sweat trade chatter . I think it's far too early in the season to part ways with one of their best players.
However, a quarterback trade wouldn't be completely out of the picture. The Cardinals have a fairly thick room with Jacoby Brissett set to be the starter and Gardner Minshew/Carson Beck also in the mix. Arizona just might want to depart from Minshew and have Beck waiting in the wings if they want to make a change.
Trey Benson would have been a prime candidate here before his release.
How likely? I'd say they might not be looking to acquire talent at the moment. Maybe a 3 out of 10 on the scale.
I've always been pretty confident Love would rebound in time for Week 1, though I am just a tad skeptical on his full availability/workload.
Love seems to be progressing well after suffering a (reported) high ankle sprain in Las Vegas. Make what you want of him working out barefoot in Green Bay after carrying loads of pizza on the team plane for rookie duties.
I do think Love will be ready to go, though the Cardinals will probably want to be smart on working him back into the mix with a pitch count in Week 1.
This sort of ties into the trade question above, though I don't think the Cardinals are exactly positioned as buyers entering the season.
Defensively, they just want to see their unit healthy. Arizona barely played their starters in preseason, and while Nick Rallis is considered to have a short leash in 2026, he does have an opportunity to wipe the slate clean and start anew without Jonathan Gannon in the building.
Arizona opted to mostly upgrade the offensive side of the ball this offseason. It's a bet they're hoping pays off under the offensive-minded LaFleur.
I do think with Wilson, Harrison and Bourne in the mix we were likely to see plenty of 11 personnel from the Cardinals, but oddly enough I'm not sure Reiman's injury will really prevent LaFleur from wanting to run those coveted multi-TE sets.
Reiman's undoubtedly their best in-line blocker at the position, though Teagan Quitoriano is fairly strong in that department. It's not a one-for-one fill in, though the Cardinals (under my belief) still would like to get heavy.
Even the Rams' usage of 11 personnel last year was slightly above the league average, so if LaFleur carries over any of Sean McVay's philosophy, we should still see it often.
Bryan, the Cardinals' offense has — operationally — looked sound and solid this camp/preseason. Has it been perfect?
Not quite, though when all three levels of the offense are operating at a high level, regardless of the quarterback, that's an incredibly encouraging sign that LaFleur's offense is not only digestible but effective, too.
Another positive has been the uptick in health of Arizona's starters. The Cardinals have recently gotten back Garrett Williams and Josh Sweat while Walter Nolen III has managed to stay healthy. The Cardinals need all hands on deck when it comes to their defense, and that's exactly what they're getting as preseason comes to a close.
JDUBZ, that's an excellent question.
Nobody really knows what's going on with James Conner right now. He hit injured reserve after suffering a foot injury in Week 3 last season and hasn't played a snap of 11 v 11 football since. He's been mostly present at practice but only participating in individual drills.
The Cardinals could simply be keeping their veteran running back healthy while others suggest Conner might not be ready to play just yet. Arizona's done a great job of keeping their intentions sealed.
To answer your question, Conner probably doesn't have a lot of value in terms of a trade, but the Cardinals would like to get something of value in return if he's going to leave. That being said, Conner's earned the right and respect from the organization to be released if that's his wish.
I think with three running backs already in the mix, Conner has a slightly better chance of being cut than traded — especially since that would allow him to choose his own team.

title: Cardinals Final 53-Man Roster Prediction: Does James Conner Make the Cut?
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals will be trimming their roster nearly in half come Sunday.
All that stands between general manager Monti Ossenfort and establishing a 53-man roster is Friday's preseason battle against the Green Bay Packers — and a few days of evaluation.
For now, here's our best shot at the 53-man roster:
The Cardinals, unless a trade involving Gardner Minshew arises , will be forced to keep three quarterbacks on their active roster to begin the season. It would be a bit of a surprise to see that number remain through the end of the regular season.
This was a tough decision to keep four, though with Arizona's intention to run the ball early and often under LaFleur, the organization keeps Knight in case of injury and special teams prowess. This decision is made easier thanks to Trey Benson's move to IR.
Jalen Brooks or Ihmir Smith-Marsette could slot into a sixth spot here, though one (if not both) could clear waivers and be brought back to the practice squad. Duvernay's value as a returner solidified his roster spot while Virgil showed promise as a fifth-round rookie.
It's very possible Tip Reiman starts on Reserve/PUP to begin the season, as it doesn't appear he's close to returning. If that's the case, Arizona still rolls with a deep tight end room with plenty of 12 and 13 personnel on the horizon.
The expected starting five is here with a mix of guards/tackles behind them. Oli Udoh or Matt Pryor could sneak in here, though we feel good about two backups each for interior and exterior offensive line spots. Gaines' versatility to also play center is key.
This feels like a fairly light defensive line room, as Nick Rallis loves to rotate his front during games. However, outside of these six, it's tough to justify another talent in the room — especially with other positions requiring more roster spots.
This could qualify as the biggest surprise of the roster with no BJ Ojulari listed, though the veteran has been disappointing in camp/preseason while Leota has improved his stock enough to warrant the spot over Ojulari — especially with Sweat now back in the picture .
The Cardinals could very well keep five inside linebackers, though Owen Pappoe loses out of the race to Sharar simply due to Sharar's status as a recent draft pick that's impressed on special teams.
Williams' activation from PUP gives the Cardinals their slot corner back in the mix, which pushes a talented player out of the room. The last spot that Thomas occupies could very well go to somebody like Kei'Trel Clark, who previously started games in the desert.
With Joey Blount landing on injured reserve, the safety room now feels pretty comfortable in terms of identifying both depth and pecking order. The Cardinals seem to be comfortable with everybody here.

title: Cardinals WR Michael Wilson Reveals Surprising Beef With Packers Corner
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals WR Michael Wilson is one of the most genuine athletes you'll come across.
In a world full of attention and social media, Wilson mostly opts to lay low. Forget about a slice of humble pie — Wilson's practically the entire thing.
So to discover Wilson has beef with anybody in the league, it's a bit surprising.
Wilson and Green Bay Packers cornerback Keisean Nixon apparently aren't fond of each other. That was evident in today's joint practice , where the two got in each other's faces after Wilson picked up a first down — which prompted a bench-clearing brawl.
Benches clear again as Michael Wilson picks up a first down and benches clear again as Wilson and Packers Keisean Nixon get in each others face. 3 times we’ve had benches clear by my count.
Wilson, speaking with reporters after the practice, didn't quite mince words on Nixon:
"Me and him got a little bit of beef going back to my second year in the league. Every time I see him - I'm not going to say it's smoke - but not too fond of him and I don't think he's too fond of me. I'll just leave it at that," he said per Arizona Sports' Tyler Drake.
Michael Wilson not sugarcoating things when talking about Packers CB Keisean Nixon to reporters following their scuffle at joint practice: "Me and him got a little bit of beef going back to my second year in the league. Every time I see him - I'm not going to say it's smoke -…
Wilson's referring to the Cardinals' 34-13 Week 6 loss to Green Bay back in 2024, where he caught two passes for 21 yards and a touchdown. Nixon had three tackles and one pass defensed.
Wilson, entering his fourth season in the league, is fresh off his first 1,000-yard receiving campaign and hopes to expand his role even further under new head coach Mike LaFleur.
As Mark McClune suggested in his X post above, there were a handful of flare-ups in today's joint practice. While none seemed to get out of control, the competitive juices were certainly flowing.
Nixon, oddly enough, is from Los Angeles but played for two seasons at Arizona Western (located in Yuma) before transferring to South Carolina to finish his collegiate career.
The Packers and Cardinals aren't set to play each other this coming regular season, so a potential Wilson vs. Nixon battle will have to wait for 2027 or beyond.
“You guys have that green and gold, but to me, Cardinal red is the best color in football," Wilson added after practice.

title: Falcons Trade Rumor: Tua Tagovailoa Drawing Interest as QB Battle Reaches Final Stage
full_text:
The Atlanta Falcons are entering their final preseason game with plenty of questions surrounding the quarterback position, and a new report has added another layer of intrigue to the competition.
Denver Broncos reporter Benjamin Allbright reported Thursday afternoon that multiple quarterbacks could be on the move in the coming weeks. Among the names he listed as receiving interest around the league were Falcons quarterback Tua Tagovailoa, along with Dillon Gabriel, J.J. McCarthy, and Anthony Richardson.
“Could see multiple QBs on the move in the next few weeks,” Allbright wrote. “All have had calls placed on them to varying degrees of interest.”
Could see multiple QBs on the move in the next few weeks. -Tua -Gabriel -McCarthy -Richardson All have had calls placed on them to varying degrees of interest.
The report does not indicate that the Falcons are actively shopping Tagovailoa, nor does it suggest a trade is imminent. It does, however, establish that there has been outside interest in the veteran quarterback as teams around the league evaluate their quarterback situations before the regular season.
For Atlanta, the timing is notable.
Tagovailoa will start Friday night against the Miami Dolphins in the Falcons’ preseason finale at Hard Rock Stadium. Michael Penix Jr. will not play as he continues working his way back from an ACL injury, while Kevin Stefanski continues to evaluate the quarterback competition.
The Falcons signed Tagovailoa this offseason to compete with Penix for the starting job, but the competition has remained unsettled. Penix had been limited during the early portion of training camp while recovering from his injury, and Tagovailoa missed the first week of training camp with a back injury.
Penix was cleared for 11-on-11 work earlier this week, marking the beginning of what was expected to be the true competition between the two quarterbacks.
However, Penix potentially winning the job remains very much in play because Tagovailoa has not separated himself from the former first-round pick in his limited time on the field.
That makes Friday’s game particularly important for Tagovailoa. While Penix will not have another preseason opportunity to make his case, Tagovailoa will have the chance to show Stefanski why he should be the team’s Week 1 starter in two weeks against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
The Falcons have set no deadline to name their starter for the Steelers game, with Stefanski joking that he’ll wait as long as the league allows him.
“Whenever they tell me I have to,” Stefanski said this week. “Honestly, not trying to be coy. Just a little focus on what's available to us, what information is available to us. Obviously, this has been something that we need to work through as people come back off of injury. I mean, Tua was injured to start camp, and then Mike's been injured, not doing the 11-on-11. So, you just every day you're just trying to make decisions based on who's available to you. The good news is very, very happy with our guys and the progress they've all made.”
If Tagovailoa performs well against his former team, the trade rumors could quickly become secondary to his pursuit of the starting job and give the Falcons the luxury of giving Penix more time to recover from his surgery. If he struggles, however, the possibility of Atlanta ultimately choosing Penix becomes even more likely.
For now, Tagovailoa remains a Falcon and is scheduled to start Friday night . But with teams reportedly calling and the Falcons still searching for clarity at quarterback, his situation is one worth monitoring as the regular season approaches.

title: Falcons vs. Dolphins Odds, How to Watch for Preseason Week 3
full_text:
MIAMI – The Atlanta Falcons are putting a bow on the 2026 preseason slate on Friday night with a trip to Miami to take on the Miami Dolphins, and there is still a lot on the line coming into this game.
The quarterback competition reached a new level with the medical clearance of Michael Penix Jr., but Kevin Stefanski disappointed many when he announced Tuesday that the incumbent starter would remain sidelined for this game. Tua Tagovailoa, on the other hand, is set to take on his former team with everything on the line.
The former Dolphins quarterback has struggled this summer in Penix's absence, but the third preseason game will be another important milestone in his quest to take the Falcons’ Week 1 starting job. How he performs in this game could make or break those chances.
In the absence of Penix, Cooper Rush and Jack Strand will both look to match their outstanding Week 2 performances as they battle for the third quarterback slot on the roster.
Elsewhere, it remains to be seen who will suit up for Atlanta. Stefanski opted to play many of his offensive linemen for the first preseason game, but Jake Matthews exited with an undisclosed injury, and Jawaan Taylor remained sidelined with his knee injury. Friday could be the first time we see the new right tackle, but that remains to be seen.
Bijan Robinson and Drake London, meanwhile, did not play. Several prominent defenders also did not play, but it is unclear which of those players may or may not suit up Friday night.
“One of the things that you learn from the data that medical provides you is how much you should do, what playing in these games, what playing in joint practices does to your first few weeks of the season from a soft tissue perspective, which I believe in,” Stefanski explained earlier this week.
“There's great data that was shared with us at the league meetings, and we've tried to follow through on a lot of that. So, getting X number of plays in preseason, getting to joint practices, I think sets you up for success in the fall. It's not a guarantee of anything, but it does set you up. So, we have a plan.”
The Falcons will not get all the answers during this game, but it is the final audition for the competitions throughout the roster. The numbers on the scoreboard may not matter, but the performances on the field may matter more now than ever.
